regions.name: Czech Silesia (Ostrava)
regions.identity_basis: A remnant of the historic Duchy of (Czech/Austrian) Silesia, administratively distinct from both Bohemia and Moravia; a heavy coal/steel industrial identity (Ostrava-Karviná coal basin, Vítkovice steelworks) plus a genuine Polish national minority in the Zaolzie/Těšín Silesia area straddling the Czech-Polish border. Twinned with pl-silesia across the border in the new "silesia" variant set (data/variant_sets/zone67.json): the "current" view shows both as separate congruent-with-current-states records (unchanged here); a "connected" view shows a unified silesia-unified region (default_visible false) spanning both.
regions.population_note: Eurostat/CZSO 2023 estimate for Moravskoslezský kraj (CZ08).

pole.note: Ostrava dominates the Karviná-Havířov conurbation.

conflict_flags.description: Polish national minority in the Zaolzie/Těšín Silesia area on the Czech side of the historic Cieszyn Silesia partition — a cross-border Silesian-identity layer distinct from the Moravian census self-identification recorded elsewhere in Czechia.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Ostrava — metro ~1.0M with the Karviná-Havířov conurbation, Czechia's 3rd-largest urban agglomeration
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: coal (declining, EU just-transition region), steel, automotive supply (near the Hyundai Nošovice plant), engineering
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: a distinct Silesian regional-administrative identity (kept as Moravskoslezský kraj rather than folded into a Moravian kraj); a genuine Polish-minority Zaolzie/Těšín Silesia layer, historically contested between Poland and Czechoslovakia (1919-20, 1938)

regions.nuts1_disagreement: Czechia's NUTS-1 (CZ0) treats the whole country as one unit; the Czech NUTS-2 level itself already keeps Moravskoslezský separate from the Jihovýchod/Střední Morava kraje we group as 'Moravia' — we follow that existing administrative distinction rather than inventing a new one.
regions.lang_family: West Slavic (Czech; Polish minority in Zaolzie/Těšín Silesia)

autarky.rationale: Historic coal self-sufficiency is winding down under EU just-transition funding, mirroring Polish Upper Silesia across the border, keeping energy only moderate; dense post-industrial land use constrains shelter; cross-border road/rail links to Poland support transportation.

rationales.water: Odra-basin water access, industrially stressed, mirroring Polish Upper Silesia across the border.
rationales.food: Average food self-sufficiency; dense industrial land use leaves little room for agriculture.
rationales.energy: Historic coal self-sufficiency is winding down under EU just-transition funding, mirroring Polish Upper Silesia across the border, keeping energy only moderate.
rationales.transportation: Cross-border road/rail links to Poland support transportation.

sources: EU Just Transition Fund Moravskoslezský programme
Zahra (2008) on the Cieszyn Silesia partition

regions.name: Silesia (unified, PL+CZ)
regions.identity_basis: Unified-view record for the "silesia" variant set (like tyrol-unified): historic Upper+Czech Silesia (Duchy of Silesia, later Prussian/Austrian partition) reunited across the modern Polish-Czech border, spanning the same coal/steel industrial basin and Ślązacy/Silesian-ethnolect continuum on both sides. Shown only in the "connected" and "overlap" views; the "current" (default) view shows pl-silesia and cz-czech-silesia separately, reflecting today's state borders.
regions.population_note: Sum of pl-silesia (5,240,000) and cz-czech-silesia (1,170,000).

pole.note: Two comparably-weighted coal-basin conurbations, historically one Duchy of Silesia, now split by the Polish-Czech border; neither side is subordinate to the other.

parliament.note: No cross-border legislature exists; this is a cultural/historical unified view only, not a governance proposal.

conflict_flags.description: The historic Duchy of Silesia was partitioned between Prussia/Germany and Austria-Hungary/Czechoslovakia; today's Polish-Czech border bisects a continuous coal/steel industrial basin and Silesian-ethnolect dialect continuum. Shown as a toggleable unified view, not a territorial claim.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Katowice/Ostrava — combined conurbation >3M across the border
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: coal, steel, automotive, chemicals on both sides of the border
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: cross-border cultural/ethnolinguistic continuity; this unified view is a cultural-mapping exercise, not a political claim — both Poland and Czechia keep their Silesian populations firmly within the national state

regions.nuts1_disagreement: Spans two countries' NUTS-1/2 systems (PL5/PL22/PL52 and CZ08); this is a noncongruent unified record analogous to tyrol-unified.
regions.lang_family: West Slavic (Polish/Czech; shared Silesian ethnolect continuum)

autarky.rationale: A straightforward sum of the two congruent-view records' profiles; the cross-border coal-basin economy reads as one system on the ground even though governed by two states.

rationales.water: Odra-basin water access on both sides of the border, industrially stressed.
rationales.food: Average food self-sufficiency; dense cross-border industrial land use.
rationales.energy: Combined coal self-sufficiency winding down under EU just-transition funding on both sides.

sources: Zahra (2008) on the Cieszyn Silesia partition

regions.name: Bratislava & Western Slovakia
regions.identity_basis: Bratislava-centered western and central Slovakia forms an integrated automotive-manufacturing corridor (Bratislava-Trnava-Nitra-Žilina) along the Váh valley. A1.8 confirms the capital-region unit explicitly INCLUDES western AND central Slovakia (SK01+SK02+SK03): Central Slovakia's Žilina and Banská Bystrica kraje, though historically the 1944 Slovak National Uprising (SNP) heartland, are drawn into this bloc on the strength of the shared automotive-industrial corridor (Kia Žilina is functionally continuous with the Bratislava-Trnava-Nitra supply chain) rather than kept as a third region — a runner-up case for a future 3-way split, flagged rather than silently erased.
key_industries: automotive manufacturing (Volkswagen Bratislava, Kia Žilina, Jaguar Land Rover Nitra, Stellantis Trnava)
regions.population_note: Sum of Bratislavský, Západné Slovensko and Stredné Slovensko NUTS-2 regions, Statistical Office of the Slovak Republic 2023 estimate.

pole.note: Bratislava is the dominant single pole, but the automotive corridor genuinely spans multiple comparable industrial cities rather than radiating purely from the capital.

parliament.name: Krajské zastupiteľstvá (Bratislavský, Trnavský, Trenčiansky, Nitriansky, Žilinský, Banskobystrický)
parliament.note: Real elected regional assemblies (samosprávne kraje) exist at kraj level; this cultural unit spans six kraje/assemblies, flagged for the CA parliament-exceptions audit.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Bratislava — metro ~660k, national capital, seat of government and EU-adjacent financial-services base
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: one of the world's highest per-capita car-production corridors (VW Bratislava, Stellantis Trnava, Kia Žilina, Jaguar Land Rover Nitra), plus electronics and finance
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: Bratislava's cosmopolitan, EU-oriented identity is distinct from the rest of Slovakia; Central Slovakia (Žilina, Banská Bystrica) carries its own real Slovak National Uprising (SNP) historical identity, which we do not split out separately here per A1.8's mandated 2-way framing

regions.nuts1_disagreement: Slovakia's NUTS-1 (SK0) is the whole country as a single unit; our split follows the country's own NUTS-2 regions grouped into two (per A1.8) rather than the four official NUTS-2 units, collapsing Stredné Slovensko into the western/capital bloc rather than retaining it as a third national region.

autarky.rationale: The automotive-manufacturing corridor supports strong transportation infrastructure (the motorway/rail spine along the Váh); Bratislava's healthcare capacity and Danube-basin water access are strong; food self-sufficiency is only moderate given how much agricultural land has shifted to industrial/logistics use.

rationales.water: Danube-basin water access is strong around Bratislava.
rationales.food: Food self-sufficiency is only moderate given how much agricultural land has shifted to industrial/logistics use.
rationales.energy: Energy draws on the national grid mix (incl. Jaslovské Bohunice/Mochovce nuclear plants nearby) but is not scored as a standalone regional generation asset.
rationales.transportation: The automotive-manufacturing corridor supports strong transportation infrastructure (the motorway/rail spine along the Váh).

sources: Statistical Office of the Slovak Republic 2023
Slovak Investment and Trade Development Agency (SARIO) automotive-sector reports

regions.name: Eastern Slovakia (Košice-Prešov)
regions.identity_basis: A1.8 SUPERSEDES the prior single-pole framing: Eastern Slovakia is modeled as a Košice-Prešov DIPOLE (the two Východné Slovensko NUTS-3 kraje, SK042 and SK041), not a Košice-dominant single region. Prešov carries the Rusyn/Ukrainian national minority (recognized minority-language status) concentrated in its northeastern districts — a distinct identity basis from Košice's steel/industrial economy; Slovakia's poorer, more agricultural east also has a significant Roma minority presence. The East Slovak dialect group is linguistically distinct from the Central/West Slovak dialects underlying standard Slovak.
key_industries: cross-border logistics (EU external border with Ukraine)
regions.population_note: Sum of Prešovský kraj (~811,000) and Košický kraj (~793,000), Statistical Office of the Slovak Republic 2023 estimate.

pole.note: Košice (steel/industrial, ~230k) and Prešov (~90k, administrative seat of the Rusyn/Ukrainian minority's cultural institutions) are a genuine dipole ~35km apart, not a single-pole region.

parliament.name: Krajské zastupiteľstvá (Košický, Prešovský)
parliament.note: Real elected regional assemblies (samosprávne kraje); this cultural unit spans two kraje, flagged for the CA parliament-exceptions audit.

conflict_flags.description: Rusyn/Ukrainian national minority concentrated in the northeastern Prešov region, with its own recognized minority-language status distinct from the Slovak national majority.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Košice-Prešov dipole — Košice ~230k city/~400k region (Slovakia's second-largest urban economy), Prešov ~90k
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: U.S. Steel Košice (one of Europe's largest integrated steelworks), a growing IT/BPO sector ('Košice IT Valley'), agriculture, EU-external-border logistics with Ukraine
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: the East Slovak dialect and a distinct Rusyn/Ukrainian and Roma minority presence (concentrated in Prešov kraj) give the region a genuinely different ethnolinguistic texture from the west; no separatism, but strong regional economic-development advocacy vis-à-vis Bratislava

regions.nuts1_disagreement: Slovakia's NUTS-1 (SK0) is the whole country as a single unit; we split East Slovakia out as its own dipole region while collapsing Stredné Slovensko into the western/capital bloc (see sk-bratislava-west), per A1.8's mandated 2-way framing.
regions.lang_family: West Slavic (Slovak, East Slovak dialect); Rusyn/Ukrainian (East Slavic) minority in Prešov region

autarky.rationale: The agricultural East Slovak lowlands support an above-average food score; energy remains import/grid-dependent, with the region's own generation limited largely to the U.S. Steel Košice cogeneration plant; the EU-external-border position adds transport friction not otherwise captured by this index.

rationales.water: Average water access; the Tisza/Bodrog river system gives adequate but unremarkable supply.
rationales.food: The agricultural East Slovak lowlands support an above-average food score.
rationales.energy: Energy remains import/grid-dependent, with the region's own generation limited largely to the U.S. Steel Košice cogeneration plant.

sources: Statistical Office of the Slovak Republic 2023
Council of Europe Framework Convention reporting on the Rusyn minority in Slovakia

regions.name: Budapest & Central Hungary
regions.identity_basis: Budapest and its Pest-county commuter belt form Hungary's single overwhelmingly dominant metropolitan region — roughly 30% of the national population and a still-larger share of GDP, media and cultural institutions concentrated in the capital ('vidék' cleavage). COVERAGE-DRIVEN EXTENSION beyond the user's literal Budapest/Pest naming: Fejér (Székesfehérvár) and Komárom-Esztergom (Tatabánya, Esztergom) are added here rather than left an orphaned remainder of the old Közép-Dunántúl NUTS-2 unit once Veszprém is reassigned to hu-balaton. Both counties sit on the M1 motorway/Danube corridor between Budapest and the Austrian/Slovak border, function economically as Budapest's western industrial-commuter periphery, and are NOT part of the 'West/Szombathely' or 'Balaton' identity — this is an honest coverage necessity, not a claim that Székesfehérvár or Esztergom are culturally 'Budapest'.
regions.population_note: Sum of Budapest (~1.68M), Pest (~1.35M), Fejér (~0.41M) and Komárom-Esztergom (~0.30M) counties, KSH 2023 estimate.

pole.note: Overwhelmingly dominant national capital; Fejér/Komárom-Esztergom are commuter-industrial periphery, not independent poles.

parliament.note: Hungarian county (megyei) assemblies were stripped of any meaningful policy-making function after 2010; Budapest itself has no separate sub-national parliament beyond its municipal government. See this file's HU push-back notes.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Budapest — metro ~3.0M (nearly a third of Hungary's population), overwhelmingly dominant national capital
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: finance/business services, ICT, government, pharmaceuticals, logistics, automotive (Suzuki Esztergom)
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: Budapest's cosmopolitan, opposition-leaning political culture is well-documented as distinct from the rest of Hungary, with no separatist dimension — dependence-within-the-state par excellence

regions.nuts1_disagreement: No longer matches HU1 (Közép-Magyarország) alone: extends into two NUTS-3 units of the former Közép-Dunántúl NUTS-2 (HU21) — Fejér and Komárom-Esztergom — for coverage, since Veszprém (the third HU21 county) moves to hu-balaton per the mandated 4-unit Hungary carve-up. This is a deliberate, stated deviation, not a silent one.

autarky.rationale: Overwhelming transport (Liszt Ferenc Airport, national rail/motorway hub) and healthcare (Semmelweis University hospital network) concentration; food self-sufficiency is the weakest score, since the capital region imports most of its food from the agricultural vidék it otherwise dominates economically.

rationales.water: Danube-basin access is abundant, though the capital's food and industrial demand strain per-capita supply less than elsewhere in the region.
rationales.food: Food self-sufficiency is the weakest score in the zone: the capital region imports most of its food from the agricultural vidék it otherwise dominates economically.
rationales.energy: Energy draws on the national grid (Paks nuclear plant, outside this unit) with no major regional generation asset of its own.
rationales.transportation: Overwhelming transport concentration (Liszt Ferenc Airport, national rail/motorway hub, Suzuki/automotive logistics corridor).
rationales.hygiene_healthcare: Semmelweis University hospital network gives the strongest healthcare concentration in Hungary.

sources: KSH (Hungarian Central Statistical Office) 2023 population estimates
Assembly of European Regions (2021), 'Regionalisation in Hungary: once again a centralised country'

regions.name: West Hungary (Győr-Szombathely)
regions.identity_basis: Historic Nyugat-Dunántúl (West Transdanubia) minus Zala (reassigned to hu-balaton per the user's explicit Balaton composition). Győr anchors a genuine automotive-export corridor (Audi Győr, one of Hungary's largest single employers) on the Vienna-Budapest axis; Szombathely (Vas county) carries its own distinct Pannonian/Austrian-facing civic identity, historically the seat of Roman Savaria and closest Hungarian city to Austria.
regions.population_note: Sum of Győr-Moson-Sopron (~453,000) and Vas (~250,000) counties, KSH 2023 estimate.

pole.note: Győr is the largest single city (Audi plant), but Szombathely (Vas county seat) and Sopron (historic border town, voted 1921 to stay in Hungary) are real secondary identity centers, not mere Győr suburbs — best-effort polycentric marking.

parliament.note: Hungarian county assemblies have no meaningful legislative function post-2010.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Győr — metro ~130k, dominant single hub of the reduced West-Hungary unit once Zala moves to hu-balaton
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: automotive export manufacturing (Audi Győr), logistics on the Vienna-Budapest transit corridor, electronics, cross-border trade with Austria
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: a real Pannonian/Austrian-facing civic identity distinct from both Budapest and the Alföld; Sopron's 1921 plebiscite to remain Hungarian (against the Treaty of Trianon's original Austria assignment) is the zone's clearest concrete evidence of a locally-salient, non-separatist regional identity choice

regions.nuts1_disagreement: Narrower than official Nyugat-Dunántúl (HU22), which also includes Zala; we move Zala to hu-balaton per the mandated Balaton composition (Somogy/Veszprém/Zala), stated here rather than silently absorbed.

autarky.rationale: The Vienna-Budapest transit corridor and Audi's export-manufacturing base support transportation and industrial employment; food and water are average; the region imports most energy and finished consumer goods, typical of Hungary's mid-sized industrial counties.

rationales.water: Danube/Rába river access is adequate, unremarkable.
rationales.food: Average food self-sufficiency; agricultural land has shifted toward automotive-industrial use around Győr.
rationales.energy: Grid/import-dependent, no major regional generation asset.
rationales.transportation: The Vienna-Budapest transit corridor and Sopron/Austria cross-border links give this unit's strongest score.

regions.name: Lake Balaton & South Transdanubia
regions.identity_basis: Composed per the user's explicit instruction that Balaton spans Somogy/Veszprém/Zala counties (verified: HU213/HU232/HU223). Once assembled, this leaves Baranya and Tolna (the remainder of the old Dél-Dunántúl NUTS-2 unit after Somogy moves here) needing a coverage home: they are geographically contiguous with Somogy (not with hu-west or hu-east-debrecen, which are non-adjacent), so we fold them in rather than orphan them. HONEST TENSION FLAGGED: the resulting unit's largest city by far is Pécs (Baranya, ~140k, UNESCO World Heritage old town, university), ~150km from the lake itself — the 'Lake Balaton' identity in the unit's name reflects the user's mandated naming and the lakeside tourism economy's cultural salience, not the unit's real urban-population center of gravity, which sits in Pécs. This mirrors the honesty already applied to hu-east-debrecen in v1: we keep the mandated name while stating plainly where it strains the inclusion test.
regions.population_note: Sum of Veszprém (~330,000), Zala (~267,000), Somogy (~290,000), Baranya (~360,000) and Tolna (~207,000) counties, KSH 2023 estimate.

pole.note: HONEST CASE: Pécs is the largest city but sits far south of the lake; Veszprém is the lake district's own administrative center. Marked polycentric rather than a single monopole to reflect this real duality rather than pretend one city organizes the whole territory.

parliament.note: Hungarian county assemblies have no meaningful legislative function post-2010.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: No single hub matches the 'Balaton' identity cleanly — Pécs (~140k) is the largest city but sits ~150km from the lake; Veszprém (~60k) is the lake district's own seat. A coverage-driven merger of two distinct sub-identities (lakeside tourism arc + South Transdanubian Pécs hinterland), stated honestly rather than glossed over.
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: lakeside tourism, wine (both Balaton-felvidék and Villány/Pécs), Pécs university-medical/pharma cluster, agriculture
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: both sub-areas (Balaton tourism belt, Pécs/South Transdanubia) are dependent, non-separatist Hungarian regional identities; no shared civic identity unites them beyond geographic contiguity and the mandated 4-unit carve-up

regions.nuts1_disagreement: Diverges from both former NUTS-2 units it draws from (Közép-Dunántúl HU21 and Dél-Dunántúl HU23): takes only Veszprém from HU21 (Fejér/Komárom-Esztergom go to hu-budapest) and Zala from the old HU22 Nyugat-Dunántúl, while taking all of the HU23 remainder (Somogy/Baranya/Tolna) once none of them fit hu-west or hu-east-debrecen contiguously.

autarky.rationale: Lake Balaton and the region's wine/agriculture give solid Water and Food scores; Pécs's university-medical cluster supports Hygiene & Healthcare; energy has no major remaining domestic asset since the Pécs-area coal/uranium mining legacy was decommissioned.

rationales.water: Lake Balaton itself and the Dráva/Danube tributaries give strong freshwater abundance.
rationales.food: Diversified wine and agricultural base (Balaton-felvidék, Villány) supports an above-average food score.
rationales.energy: No major domestic generation asset since the Pécs-Komló coal/uranium legacy industry was decommissioned; grid/import-dependent.

sources: University of Pécs regional development reports

regions.name: East Hungary (Debrecen)
regions.identity_basis: Now purely the former Alföld és Észak NUTS-1 macroregion (HU3: Észak-Magyarország + Észak-Alföld + Dél-Alföld) with no Dunántúl territory mixed in, since hu-balaton absorbs the Transdanubian remainder. Retains this file's honest v1 finding: no single dominant hub (Debrecen, Szeged, Miskolc, Nyíregyháza are comparably sized); the historic Alföld (Protestant, agrarian, Ottoman-legacy) identity is genuine but exists mainly in contradistinction to Budapest rather than as a positive regional identity of its own.
regions.population_note: Sum of Borsod-Abaúj-Zemplén, Heves, Nógrád, Hajdú-Bihar, Jász-Nagykun-Szolnok, Szabolcs-Szatmár-Bereg, Bács-Kiskun, Békés and Csongrád-Csanád counties (all of HU3), KSH 2023 estimate.

pole.note: No dominant single hub — Debrecen (Hungary's 2nd city, ~200k) is only modestly ahead of Szeged, Miskolc and Nyíregyháza; this is the same honest weak point flagged in v1, now cleaner since it no longer mixes in Transdanubian territory.

parliament.note: Hungarian county assemblies have no meaningful legislative function post-2010.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: no dominant single hub — Debrecen (~200k, Hungary's 2nd city) is only modestly ahead of Szeged, Nyíregyháza and Miskolc; this criterion is the acknowledged weak point of this region
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: a real and growing automotive/EV-battery manufacturing base (BMW Debrecen, Mercedes-Benz Kecskemét, CATL/Samsung SDI battery plants), agriculture (the Alföld/Great Plain breadbasket), pharmaceuticals
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: the 'vidék' (countryside) identity exists mainly in contradistinction to Budapest rather than as a positive regional identity of its own; the historic Alföld (Protestant, agrarian, Ottoman-legacy) identity is genuine but does not sustain organized political regionalism

regions.nuts1_disagreement: Matches Hungary's actual current NUTS-1 unit HU3 (Alföld és Észak) exactly, now that Transdanubian territory (formerly merged in as hu-videk) is split out to hu-budapest/hu-west/hu-balaton per the mandated 4-unit carve-up.

autarky.rationale: The Alföld/Great Plain breadbasket gives this region Hungary's strongest food score; energy self-sufficiency is dragged down by Hungary's near-total reliance on the single centralized Paks nuclear station plus Russian gas imports — a national, not regional, asset; transportation and healthcare infrastructure outside the handful of secondary cities are visibly thinner than in the capital.

rationales.water: The Danube-Tisza interfluve and Alföld water-management systems give a solid, if flood-management-dependent, water score.
rationales.food: The Alföld/Great Plain breadbasket gives this region Hungary's strongest food score.
rationales.energy: Dragged down by Hungary's near-total reliance on the single centralized Paks nuclear station plus Russian gas imports — a national, not regional, asset that does not raise any one region's autarky.

sources: regscience.hu, 'The rise and fall of regionalism in Hungary'
Assembly of European Regions (2021), 'Regionalisation in Hungary: once again a centralised country'

regions.name: Slovenia
regions.identity_basis: Single-unit exception per global constraints; Slovenia is treated as one region despite a genuine internal Eastern/Western statistical-region distinction (Vzhodna/Zahodna Slovenija) because it is a small, already-independent nation-state, not a sub-national identity seeking recognition within a larger state. A1.5 SUPERSEDES A1.5's own earlier amendment and the original Task-C4 dispatch: an East/West Maribor-Ljubljana variant set was drafted and explicitly REJECTED by the user twice ('small enough as it is') — DROPPED entirely, not authored even as a hidden fragment.
regions.population_note: Eurostat/SURS (Statistical Office of the Republic of Slovenia) 2023 estimate.

pole.note: Overwhelmingly dominant national capital, roughly a quarter of the national population.

parliament.name: Državni zbor (National Assembly of Slovenia)
parliament.note: Single-unit exception country: 'own parliament' here is trivially Slovenia's own national parliament, since the whole country is modeled as one cultural unit.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Ljubljana — metro ~500k (roughly a quarter of the national population), overwhelmingly dominant national capital
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: automotive supply, pharmaceuticals, Adriatic port logistics (Koper, Slovenia's only sea port), tourism, electronics/appliances (Gorenje)
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: not applicable — single-unit exception; Slovenia's own sub-national identity is expressed at the level of the nation-state itself, not a region within it

regions.nuts1_disagreement: None — SI0 is simultaneously the NUTS-1 unit and (via SI03/SI04) the only country in this zone with an internal NUTS-2 East/West statistical split, which we deliberately do not use, consistent with the global single-unit exception AND the user's explicit A1.5 rejection of a Maribor/Ljubljana variant set.

autarky.rationale: Alpine water resources and the Port of Koper give reasonable water/transport scores; food self-sufficiency is moderate given Slovenia's mountainous terrain; energy draws on a mix of the shared Krško nuclear plant (co-owned with Croatia), hydro and coal, kept at a middling score to reflect this shared-asset complexity.

rationales.water: Alpine water resources give a solid, above-average score.
rationales.food: Food self-sufficiency is moderate given Slovenia's mountainous terrain.
rationales.energy: Energy draws on a mix of the shared Krško nuclear plant (co-owned with Croatia), hydro and coal, kept at a middling score to reflect this shared-asset complexity.

sources: Statistical Office of the Republic of Slovenia (SURS) 2023
Luka Koper port authority annual report

regions.name: Zagreb & Continental Croatia
regions.identity_basis: Zagreb overwhelmingly dominates continental (inland, Pannonian) Croatia economically, politically and culturally; Slavonia (Osijek, within Panonska Hrvatska) carries a distinct war-affected regional identity (1991-95 Homeland War frontline, including Vukovar) which we note but do not split out.
regions.population_note: Sum of Grad Zagreb, Sjeverna Hrvatska and Panonska Hrvatska NUTS-2 regions, DZS (Croatian Bureau of Statistics) 2023 estimate.

pole.note: Overwhelmingly dominant inland economic/political/cultural center.

parliament.note: Croatian županije (counties) are deconcentrated administrative units with weak elected assemblies, not legislative parliaments — per the explicit HR/RO/BG audit rule.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Zagreb — metro ~1.1M, national capital and overwhelmingly dominant inland economic center
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: finance/ICT/pharma (Zagreb), agriculture/food processing (Slavonia's Pannonian plain), automotive supply, logistics on the Budapest-Zagreb-Adriatic corridor
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: Croatian national identity centered on the capital; Slavonia's distinct post-war reconstruction identity (Vukovar as a national symbol of the Homeland War) is a genuine sub-layer we note rather than split out

regions.nuts1_disagreement: Croatia's NUTS-1 (HR0) is the whole country as a single unit; we split it four ways (this region, Istria, Rijeka, Dalmatia) per A1.9. Slavonia/Panonska Hrvatska's own distinct war-era identity remains a candidate for a future fifth split, flagged rather than implemented here.

autarky.rationale: Slavonia's Pannonian plain agriculture gives this region Croatia's best food self-sufficiency outside Dalmatia's coastal fisheries; Zagreb's hospital/university complex supports healthcare; energy is a mixed grid/hydro/gas position, unremarkable.

rationales.water: Average, adequate Sava/Drava river-basin access.
rationales.food: Slavonia's Pannonian plain agriculture gives this region Croatia's best food self-sufficiency outside Dalmatia's coastal fisheries.
rationales.energy: Mixed grid/hydro/gas position, unremarkable.

sources: Croatian Bureau of Statistics (DZS) 2023 population estimates
Croatian Chamber of Economy Slavonia agriculture reports

regions.name: Rijeka & Kvarner
regions.identity_basis: A1.9 SUPERSEDES the prior Istria-Rijeka merger: Rijeka/Kvarner is now its OWN unit. Rijeka is Croatia's principal cargo port with a distinct Fiuman/multicultural Habsburg-Italian-Croatian-Hungarian heritage (the city was a Hungarian corpus separatum 1868-1918, then contested Italian/Yugoslav territory 1918-1947) — a civic identity genuinely separate from both Istria's bilingual regionalism and Dalmatia's coastal-Venetian identity.
key_industries: maritime port and shipping (Rijeka, Croatia's principal cargo port)
regions.population_note: Primorsko-goranska županija, DZS 2023 estimate.

pole.note: Rijeka dominates the Kvarner Gulf; no comparable secondary city.

parliament.note: Croatian županije are deconcentrated administrative units, not legislative parliaments.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Rijeka — metro ~245k, Croatia's principal cargo port and third-largest city
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: port/maritime logistics, shipbuilding (Rijeka's historic 3. Maj shipyard), Kvarner-coast tourism (Opatija)
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: a distinct Fiuman/multicultural Habsburg-Italian-Croatian-Hungarian civic heritage (corpus separatum under Hungary 1868-1918, contested Italian/Yugoslav city 1918-1947); no separatism today

regions.nuts1_disagreement: Croatia's NUTS-2 (HR03 'Jadranska Hrvatska') merges Rijeka with Istria and Dalmatia; we split at the county (NUTS-3) level three ways per A1.9, isolating Rijeka's distinct Fiuman/port-city profile from both Istria's bilingual regionalism and Dalmatia's coastal identity.
regions.lang_family: South Slavic (Croatian; historic Fiuman/Italian-influenced urban dialect)

autarky.rationale: Rijeka's cargo port and cross-border road/rail links to Slovenia/Italy support transportation; Kvarner-coast tourism and fisheries are real but modest; energy is import-dependent with no major domestic generation asset in the region itself.

rationales.water: Adequate coastal/karst water access, comparable to the rest of Adriatic Croatia.
rationales.food: Small-scale Kvarner agriculture and fisheries; modest, not a major producer.
rationales.energy: Import-dependent with no major domestic generation asset in the region itself.
rationales.transportation: Rijeka's cargo port and cross-border road/rail links to Slovenia/Italy support transportation.

sources: Port of Rijeka Authority annual report

regions.name: Istria
regions.identity_basis: A1.9 SUPERSEDES the prior Istria-Rijeka merger: Istria is now its OWN unit, isolating its genuine bilingual Croatian-Italian regional identity (a recognized Italian national minority, with officially bilingual signage/institutions in coastal Istrian towns) and its own strong regionalist political tradition (Istrian Democratic Assembly, IDS/DDI, historically the region's dominant party, advocating regional autonomy within Croatia) from Rijeka's separately-identified Fiuman port-city heritage.
regions.population_note: Istarska županija, DZS 2023 estimate.

pole.note: Pula is the largest city, but Istria's tourism/civic geography is genuinely spread across several comparably-important coastal towns (Poreč, Rovinj, Umag) rather than radiating from one center.

parliament.note: Croatian županije are deconcentrated administrative units, not legislative parliaments — though Istria's IDS/DDI-led county government exercises unusually assertive regional-autonomy advocacy relative to other Croatian counties, worth flagging for the CA audit as a borderline case.

conflict_flags.description: Recognized Italian national minority in Istria with official bilingual status (Croatian-Italian) in coastal towns, and a distinct regionalist political tradition (IDS/DDI) advocating autonomy within Croatia.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Pula — metro ~90k, Istria's largest city and historic Roman/Venetian/Austro-Hungarian naval-port center
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: tourism (dominant), agriculture (olive oil, wine, truffles), fishing, light manufacturing
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: Istria's regionalist political tradition (IDS/DDI) and recognized Italian minority give this the strongest organized sub-national political identity in Croatia, seeking greater autonomy within Croatia, not independence

regions.nuts1_disagreement: Croatia's NUTS-2 (HR03 'Jadranska Hrvatska') merges Istria with Rijeka and Dalmatia; we split at the county (NUTS-3) level three ways per A1.9, isolating Istria's distinct bilingual/regionalist profile from both Rijeka and Dalmatia.
regions.lang_family: South Slavic (Croatian); recognized Italian national minority (bilingual coastal towns)

autarky.rationale: Istrian olive/wine agriculture is diversified but small-scale; tourism dominates the economy; energy is import-dependent with no major domestic generation asset in the region itself; transportation is more modest without Rijeka's cargo-port role now split out separately.

rationales.water: Adequate karst/coastal water access, tourism-season-strained like the rest of Adriatic Croatia.
rationales.food: Istrian olive/wine/truffle agriculture is diversified but small-scale.
rationales.energy: Import-dependent with no major domestic generation asset.

sources: Council of Europe Framework Convention reporting on the Italian minority in Istria

regions.name: Dalmatia (Split)
regions.identity_basis: Historic Dalmatia, a distinct Adriatic-coast cultural region with its own dialect (Chakavian/Dalmatian coastal speech with Venetian-Italian influence), Venetian-era architectural heritage, and a strong regional identity ('Dalmatinac' as a self-description distinct from 'kontinentalac'/inlander) within Croatia. Unchanged in composition by A1.9 (which added hr-rijeka as a new unit split off the old hr-istria-rijeka, not from this record); Lika (Ličko-senjska županija, HR032) stays here as before, though it is geographically closer to Rijeka's hinterland than to coastal Dalmatia — flagged as a candidate for a future reassignment to hr-rijeka rather than silently perfected.
regions.population_note: Sum of Zadarska, Šibensko-kninska, Splitsko-dalmatinska, Dubrovačko-neretvanska and Ličko-senjska counties (županije), DZS 2023 estimate.

pole.note: Split dominates as Croatia's second city and the Adriatic coast's largest urban/cultural center.

parliament.note: Croatian županije are deconcentrated administrative units, not legislative parliaments.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Split — metro ~450k (Splitsko-dalmatinska county), Croatia's second city and the Adriatic coast's largest urban/cultural center
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: tourism (dominant), maritime shipping and fisheries, wine/olive agriculture, construction — genuine seasonality risk noted in the autarky rationale below
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: distinct Dalmatian regional identity and dialect within Croatia, expressed through strong local self-identification and folk-cultural institutions (e.g. klapa singing); no separatism

regions.nuts1_disagreement: Croatia's NUTS-1 (HR0) is a single unit; even NUTS-2 (HR03 'Jadranska Hrvatska'/Adriatic Croatia) merges Dalmatia with Istria and Rijeka — we split at the NUTS-3 (county) level specifically to separate Dalmatia from Istria and (per A1.9) Rijeka. Ličko-senjska (Lika) stays attached here per v1 rather than moving to hr-rijeka, unreviewed for A1.9 — see identity_basis caveat.
regions.lang_family: South Slavic (Croatian; Chakavian/Dalmatian coastal dialect with Venetian-Italian influence)

autarky.rationale: Summer tourism triples the resident population and puts acute seasonal stress on water supply and healthcare capacity, the two lowest-scoring dimensions alongside energy (near-total import dependence, no major domestic generation); Adriatic fisheries and Dalmatian hinterland viticulture support a moderate food score.

rationales.water: Summer tourism triples the resident population and puts acute seasonal stress on water supply, the lowest-scoring dimension alongside energy.
rationales.food: Adriatic fisheries and Dalmatian hinterland viticulture support a moderate food score.
rationales.energy: Near-total import dependence, no major domestic generation asset.

sources: Croatian National Tourist Board seasonal-visitor statistics

regions.name: Transylvania
regions.identity_basis: Historic autonomous principality (14th-1867) inside the Hungarian/Habsburg sphere; Transylvanian Saxon heritage over a Romanian Orthodox/Greek-Catholic majority; distinct 'Ardelean' civic identity, dialect features, and Austro-Hungarian-era urban fabric set it apart from Wallachia and Moldavia within a united, non-separatist Romania. A1.12 SUPERSEDES the v0.1.0 conflict_flag-only treatment: Covasna, Harghita and Mureș (the Székely-Hungarian-majority/plurality counties) are now carved OUT as their own visible cultural unit, ro-szekely-land — this record's territory and NUTS-3 code list shrink accordingly (Alba, Brașov, Sibiu remain from the old Centru NUTS-2, plus all of Nord-Vest).
regions.population_note: Sum of Nord-Vest (RO11, ~2.59M: Bihor/Bistrița-Năsăud/Cluj/Maramureș/Satu Mare/Sălaj) plus Alba/Brașov/Sibiu (~1.26M, the Centru remainder once Covasna/Harghita/Mureș move to ro-szekely-land), Institutul Național de Statistică (INS) 2021 census; approximate, rounded.

pole.note: Cluj-Napoca is the largest single cultural/tech hub, but Brașov and Sibiu are genuinely comparable secondary Transylvanian cities, not mere satellites.

parliament.note: Romanian județe (counties) are deconcentrated administrative units with weak elected councils, not legislative parliaments — per the explicit HR/RO/BG audit rule.

conflict_flags.description: Székely Land / Hungarian-minority overlay retained per the mandated instruction even though the territory is now its own visible unit (ro-szekely-land): this flag marks the historic Transylvania-wide Hungarian/Saxon minority layer that predates and exceeds the modern Covasna/Harghita/Mureș county boundaries (e.g. Cluj and Târgu Mureș itself have long-standing Hungarian urban populations outside the three carved-out counties).

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Cluj-Napoca — metro >400k, largest non-capital cultural/university hub in Romania
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: IT/software, automotive supply, furniture, machinery, viticulture
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: strong regional identity and dialect distinctness within Romania; no separatist movement at the (now-narrower) Transylvania-proper level

regions.nuts1_disagreement: Previously matched RO1 (Nord-Vest + Centru) as one aggregate code; now authored as explicit NUTS-3 codes since Covasna/Harghita/Mureș (part of Centru/RO12) move to ro-szekely-land per A1.12 — the aggregate RO1 code no longer describes this record's true territory.
regions.lang_family: Eastern Romance (Romanian); historic Transylvanian Saxon (German) heritage minority

autarky.rationale: Carpathian water/forestry base and diversified food production keep Water/Food solid; strong road/rail hub at Cluj lifts Transportation; industrial base is real but mid-scale, capping Energy and Clothing.

rationales.water: Carpathian water/forestry base keeps this solid across the shrunk territory.
rationales.food: Diversified food production (Alba/Sibiu agriculture, Nord-Vest orchards) keeps this solid.
rationales.energy: Industrial base is real but mid-scale, capping energy self-sufficiency; no major regional generation asset.
rationales.transportation: Strong road/rail hub at Cluj lifts transportation.

sources: Institutul Național de Statistică (INS) — Recensământul Populației și Locuințelor 2021
Livezeanu, I. (1995) Cultural Politics in Greater Romania: Regionalism, Nation Building and Ethnic Struggle, 1918-1930 (Cornell UP)

regions.name: Székely Land
regions.identity_basis: A1.12 mandate: Covasna, Harghita and (with a caveat) Mureș counties carved OUT of Transylvania as their own visible cultural unit. Covasna and Harghita have Hungarian-speaking (Székely) super-majorities (~73% and ~85% respectively per the 2021 census); Mureș is more ethnically mixed (~38% Hungarian, plurality but not majority, concentrated in Târgu Mureș and its Székely hinterland) — included per the user's explicit RO12x instruction but flagged honestly as the unit's weakest-fit county. A live, organized Székely autonomy movement (Szekler National Council, Székely flag, periodic autonomy-day marches) exists, seeking territorial autonomy WITHIN Romania, not independence — this sits close to but does not cross the inclusion test's third-criterion line (dependent, not separatist), an honest tension worth flagging given how much stronger this autonomy movement is than any other in this file's zone.
regions.population_note: Sum of Covasna (~192,000), Harghita (~286,000) and Mureș (~510,000) counties, INS 2021 census; approximate.

pole.note: No single Székely capital historically (the medieval 'Székely seats' were plural); Târgu Mureș is by far the largest city but is more ethnically mixed than the historic Székely core towns Miercurea Ciuc and Sfântu Gheorghe — honest polycentric marking rather than a false single monopole.

parliament.note: No legally-recognized Székely Land parliament or autonomous assembly currently exists in Romanian law — the Szekler National Council is a civil-society/advocacy body, not a constituted legislature. This is precisely why, per the parliament-rule's own logic, Székely Land does NOT get a standalone representation grouping the way Vojvodina (a real constitutional assembly) does — see data/groupings/zone67.json rationale.

conflict_flags.description: Live, organized Székely/Hungarian territorial-autonomy movement (Szekler National Council; periodic autonomy-day demonstrations; own flag) seeking self-government within Romania. Romania's central government has consistently rejected territorial-autonomy proposals; no legal Székely Land entity exists. Shown as an identity/political layer on this unit, not a redrawn or seceded territory.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Târgu Mureș (~130k, largest city but ethnically mixed, not purely Székely) vs. the smaller, more homogeneously Székely seats Miercurea Ciuc (~38k) and Sfântu Gheorghe (~50k) — a genuine three-way split rather than one dominant hub
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: agriculture/dairy, forestry, heritage tourism, modest light manufacturing in Târgu Mureș — thinner industrial diversification than Transylvania proper
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: an active, organized autonomy-seeking movement exists (Szekler National Council) — closer to the separatism/autonomy line than any other unit in this dataset, though it stops short of independence claims and Romania's constitution and courts have repeatedly rejected the territorial-autonomy proposals; retained as dependent-not-seeking-independence but flagged as this file's most contested application of that criterion

regions.nuts1_disagreement: Carved out of the old RO1/RO12 (Centru) aggregate per A1.12; verified NUTS-3 codes RO123 (Covasna), RO124 (Harghita), RO125 (Mureș) against both nuts_index.json and the GISCO raw geometry file.
regions.lang_family: Uralic (Hungarian, Székely sub-dialect) super-majority in Covasna/Harghita; plurality in Mureș alongside Romanian

autarky.rationale: A genuine Székely pastoral/dairy agricultural tradition and Carpathian water resources support Water and Food; the region is otherwise Romania's most rural in this file's Transylvanian cluster, with thinner Shelter, Transportation and Hygiene & Healthcare infrastructure than Cluj-anchored Transylvania proper.

rationales.water: Carpathian headwaters (Târnava, Olt sources) give solid freshwater access.
rationales.food: Genuine dairy/agriculture base (Székely traditional pastoral economy) supports a solid food score.
rationales.energy: No major regional generation asset; grid/import-dependent, a modest rural economy overall.

sources: Institutul Național de Statistică (INS) — Recensământul Populației și Locuințelor 2021
Bottoni, S. (2018) Stalin's Legacy in Romania: The Hungarian Autonomous Region

regions.name: Banat (Timișoara)
regions.identity_basis: Banat (RO42) is real at its Timișoara-Timiș-Caraș-Severin core but weaker at its edges: Arad county is transitional Banat/Crișana and Hunedoara county is arguably more Transylvanian (iron-and-coal Hunedoara/Hațeg belt) than Banatian. We keep the mandated split and the NUTS-2 RO42 boundary (the only cleanly resolvable option) rather than inventing an unresolvable sub-county carve-out; the mandate is stronger in its core than at its administrative edges.
regions.population_note: Vest (RO42) NUTS-2 region, INS 2021 census.

pole.note: Timișoara dominates; Arad and Reșița are clearly secondary.

parliament.note: Romanian județe are deconcentrated administrative units, not legislative parliaments.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Timișoara — metro ~330k, Romania's 3rd city, historic multi-ethnic Habsburg administrative seat
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: automotive/electronics components, agriculture, engineering, growing IT sector
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: genuine Banat regional identity, strongest at the Timișoara-Timiș-Caraș-Severin core; weaker at the Arad (transitional) and formerly-included Hunedoara (more Transylvanian) edges, honestly noted

regions.nuts1_disagreement: Uses the NUTS-2 RO42 boundary as the only cleanly resolvable option even though Banat's cultural core (Timiș/Caraș-Severin) is narrower than the full RO42 (which also includes Arad and Hunedoara) — the mandate is honored at the administrative level available.
regions.lang_family: Eastern Romance (Romanian); historic Banat Swabian (German), Serbian and Hungarian minority heritage

autarky.rationale: Danube-Carpathian mixed farming and river resources keep Water/Food solid; a genuine industrial base (automotive, electronics) supports Transportation, but the region imports most finished consumer goods (Clothing low) and healthcare capacity concentrates in Timișoara, thinning Hygiene & Healthcare elsewhere.

rationales.water: Danube-Carpathian mixed river resources keep this solid.
rationales.food: Danube-Carpathian mixed farming keeps Food solid.
rationales.energy: A genuine industrial base (automotive, electronics) supports employment but the region imports most of its energy; no major regional generation asset.
rationales.transportation: A genuine industrial base (automotive, electronics) supports Transportation infrastructure.

sources: Institutul Național de Statistică (INS) — Recensământul Populației și Locuințelor 2021

regions.name: Wallachia & Bucharest
regions.identity_basis: Historic Wallachia (Țara Românească), the pre-1859 Danubian Principality that united with Moldavia to form modern Romania; Bucharest as national 'primate city' overwhelmingly dominates, with Oltenia (Craiova, Sud-Vest) sharing the same Ottoman-vassal Wallachian historical trajectory as Sud-Muntenia.
regions.population_note: Sum of Sud-Muntenia (RO31), București-Ilfov (RO32) and Sud-Vest Oltenia (RO41), INS 2021 census.

pole.note: Overwhelmingly dominant national capital and primate city; Craiova/Ploiești/Pitești are real but clearly secondary.

parliament.note: Romanian județe are deconcentrated administrative units, not legislative parliaments; Bucharest's own municipal government is not a regional parliament in the sense used by this audit.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Bucharest — national capital, dominant metro >2.2M
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: government/finance, oil refining (Ploiești), agriculture, automotive (Dacia)
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: Romanian national identity centered on the capital; Oltenia's distinct sub-regional character is real but shares Wallachia's broader historical trajectory closely enough to justify one region

regions.nuts1_disagreement: Merges three NUTS-2 units (Sud-Muntenia, București-Ilfov, Sud-Vest Oltenia) into one historically-coherent Wallachia region, since Oltenia's identity, while real, tracks Wallachia's pre-1859 principality history rather than forming an independently mandated split.

autarky.rationale: Danube-plain agriculture (Sud-Muntenia, Oltenia grain/vegetables) supports Food; capital transport infrastructure (Bucharest hub airport, rail, metro) is the country's strongest, but the region imports most manufactured clothing and a large share of energy despite Ploiești refining capacity.

rationales.water: Danube-plain access is adequate, unremarkable relative to the capital's demand.
rationales.food: Danube-plain agriculture (Sud-Muntenia, Oltenia grain/vegetables) supports Food.
rationales.energy: The region imports a large share of energy despite Ploiești refining capacity, which processes more than it produces domestically.
rationales.transportation: Capital transport infrastructure (Bucharest hub airport, rail, metro) is the country's strongest.

sources: Institutul Național de Statistică (INS) — Recensământul Populației și Locuințelor 2021

regions.name: Moldavia & Dobrogea
regions.identity_basis: Historic Moldavia (the other pre-1859 Danubian Principality) anchored by Iași, its former capital and cultural/university center, paired here with Dobrogea (Constanța/Tulcea, Black Sea coast, only annexed to Romania in 1878) for coverage — a genuinely bipolar Moldavia-interior/Dobrogea-coast identity, honestly noted as two historically distinct areas joined for regional coverage rather than one shared civic identity.
key_industries: Black Sea port trade and shipping (Constanța)
regions.population_note: Sum of Nord-Est (RO21) and Sud-Est (RO22), INS 2021 census.

pole.note: Iași (Moldavia's historic capital/university seat) and Constanța (Romania's main Black Sea port) are genuinely separate poles of comparable regional weight, not one dominant hub.

parliament.note: Romanian județe are deconcentrated administrative units, not legislative parliaments.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Iași — metro >400k, former Moldavian capital and major university center; Constanța — Romania's main Black Sea port, comparable weight
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: agriculture, Black Sea port trade, shipbuilding (Galați), Danube Delta/coastal tourism
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: Moldavia's own historic-principality identity is real and strong at Iași; Dobrogea's Ottoman/Black-Sea coastal history and 1878 annexation date are genuinely distinct — this region is Romania's most economically lagging (Nord-Est is the EU's poorest NUTS-2 region by GDP per capita), an honest coverage-driven pairing rather than one shared identity

regions.nuts1_disagreement: Merges Nord-Est (Moldavia proper) with Sud-Est (which includes both Dobrogea's coast and Danube-plain Brăila/Galați/Buzău/Vrancea) into one region for coverage; the Moldavia/Dobrogea pairing is honestly the weaker of this file's macro-groupings on shared-identity grounds, though each half is individually strong.
regions.lang_family: Eastern Romance (Romanian); Dobrogea has a historic Turkish/Tatar Muslim minority

autarky.rationale: Fertile Moldavian plain and Danube-delta wetlands support Food; the region is Romania's most economically lagging (Nord-Est is the EU's poorest NUTS-2 region by GDP per capita), which caps Shelter, Energy and Transportation infrastructure quality outside Iași and the Constanța port corridor.

rationales.water: Danube-delta wetlands and the fertile Moldavian plain support a solid water base.
rationales.food: Fertile Moldavian plain and Danube-delta wetlands support Food strongly.
rationales.energy: Caps at a low score outside Constanța's port-adjacent processing; the region is Romania's most economically lagging (Nord-Est is the EU's poorest NUTS-2 region by GDP per capita).

sources: Institutul Național de Statistică (INS) — Recensământul Populației și Locuințelor 2021
European Commission Cohesion Report — Nord-Est GDP per capita ranking

regions.name: Sofia & West Bulgaria
regions.name_local: София и Западна България / Sofiya i Zapadna Balgariya
regions.identity_basis: Sofia as national capital dominates West Bulgaria economically and politically; Rila/Pirin mountain hinterland (Blagoevgrad) shares a Macedonian-adjacent southwestern identity.
regions.population_note: Sum of Yugozapaden NUTS-2 pre-reform correspondence (Sofia-capital + Sofia-district + Blagoevgrad + Pernik + Kyustendil), NSI (Bulgarian National Statistical Institute) 2023 estimate.

pole.note: Overwhelmingly dominant national capital.

parliament.note: Bulgarian oblasti (provinces) are deconcentrated administrative units, not legislative parliaments — per the explicit HR/RO/BG audit rule.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Sofia — national capital, dominant metro >1.2M
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: finance/ICT, government, legacy mining (Pernik)
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: Bulgarian national identity centered on the capital; no separatism

regions.nuts1_disagreement: DATA-SOURCE DISCREPANCY (see zone notes): data/nuts_index.json lists Bulgaria under a newer NUTS scheme (single NUTS-1 'BG5', NUTS-2 'BG51'-'BG54'), which does not resolve against the committed GISCO raw geometry file (pipeline/raw/NUTS_RG_20M_2024_4326.geojson), still carrying pre-reform codes (BG3/BG4 NUTS-1, BG41/BG42 etc. NUTS-2). We authored using the codes that resolve against the raw geometry, unchanged from v0.1.0.

autarky.rationale: Rila/Pirin mountain water resources are abundant; capital transport and healthcare infrastructure lead the country, but the region is a net food importer relative to the Thracian plain and imports nearly all finished clothing.

rationales.water: Rila/Pirin mountain water resources are abundant.
rationales.food: The region is a net food importer relative to the Thracian plain.
rationales.energy: No major regional generation asset; grid/import-dependent despite the capital's demand.
rationales.transportation: Capital transport infrastructure leads the country.

regions.name: Plovdiv & Thrace
regions.name_local: Пловдив и Тракия / Plovdiv i Trakiya
regions.identity_basis: The Thracian plain, Bulgaria's richest agricultural belt, anchored by Plovdiv, one of Europe's oldest continuously-inhabited cities; the Rhodope interior (Smolyan, Kardzhali) has a genuine Bulgarian-Muslim/Pomak minority layer distinct from the Thracian-plain Bulgarian-Orthodox majority.

pole.note: Plovdiv dominates the Thracian plain; the Rhodope interior towns are clearly secondary.

parliament.note: Bulgarian oblasti are deconcentrated administrative units, not legislative parliaments.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Plovdiv — metro ~675k, Bulgaria's second city
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: agriculture, textiles, tobacco, logistics
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: strong regional pride; a genuine Pomak/Turkish minority layer in the Rhodope interior, no separatism

regions.nuts1_disagreement: Same BG NUTS vintage discrepancy noted on bg-sofia-west; uses pre-reform BG42 code, which resolves against the committed GISCO raw geometry file.
regions.lang_family: South Slavic (Bulgarian); Bulgarian-Muslim (Pomak) and Turkish minority in the Rhodope interior

autarky.rationale: The Thracian plain is Bulgaria's richest agricultural belt (Food strong); textile manufacturing gives Clothing a genuine (if modest) domestic base rare among this zone's regions; the Rhodope interior (Smolyan, Kardzhali) pulls Transportation and Shelter down from Plovdiv's own higher baseline.

rationales.water: Thracian-plain river access (Maritsa basin) is abundant.
rationales.food: The Thracian plain is Bulgaria's richest agricultural belt — the zone's top food score.
rationales.energy: No major regional generation asset; grid/import-dependent despite some hydro in the Rhodope interior.
rationales.clothing: Textile manufacturing gives Clothing a genuine, if modest, domestic base.

inclusion_test.diversified_industry: tourism, port trade, oil refining (Burgas), fisheries
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: distinct coastal-trade/tourism identity from the interior grain belt, no separatism

rationales.food: Coastal fisheries and the Danube-delta edge support Food.
rationales.energy: Burgas refining gives some energy processing capacity but the region imports its crude, capping Energy.

regions.name: North Bulgaria (Danube Plain)
regions.identity_basis: Bulgaria's northern Danube-plain grain belt, Bulgaria's most economically lagging and depopulating region; Ruse ('Little Vienna', Bulgaria's main Danube river port) is the largest but not overwhelming city, alongside Pleven (WWI/liberation-war heritage) and the former medieval capital Veliko Tarnovo.
regions.population_note: Sum of pre-reform correspondence for Ruse/Pleven/Veliko Tarnovo/Vratsa/Montana/Gabrovo/Lovech/Silistra/Razgrad/Targovishte, NSI 2023 estimate.

pole.note: No single dominant city — Ruse, Pleven and Veliko Tarnovo are comparably sized, an honest reflection of this region's borderline inclusion-test status.

parliament.note: Bulgarian oblasti are deconcentrated administrative units, not legislative parliaments.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: No single dominant hub — Ruse, Pleven and Veliko Tarnovo are comparably sized; one of this zone's weaker urban-hub cases alongside gr-aegean-islands and gr-peloponnese
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: agriculture (Danube-plain grain belt), river-freight logistics, food processing — thin diversification, chronic depopulation
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: shared northern Danube-plain agrarian identity, distinct from the capital and the Black Sea coast; no separatism

regions.nuts1_disagreement: Same BG NUTS vintage discrepancy noted on bg-sofia-west; uses pre-reform BG31/BG32 codes, which resolve against the committed GISCO raw geometry file.

autarky.rationale: Danube water access and the country's grain belt keep Water/Food solid; chronic depopulation and under-investment show up directly in Shelter and Hygiene & Healthcare (rural hospital closures); Ruse's river-freight role lifts Transportation only modestly above the regional baseline.

rationales.water: Danube water access is abundant.
rationales.food: The country's grain belt keeps Food solid.
rationales.energy: Modest hydro/grid mix; no major standalone generation asset.

regions.name: Athens & Attica
regions.name_local: Αθήνα και Αττική / Athina kai Attiki
regions.identity_basis: Athens as national capital overwhelmingly dominates Greece economically, politically and culturally, with Piraeus as its port.
regions.population_note: Attiki (EL30) NUTS-2 region, ELSTAT 2021 census.

pole.note: Overwhelmingly dominant national capital.

parliament.note: Greek perifereies (regions) are deconcentrated administrative units with elected councils but not legislative parliaments — extending the HR/RO/BG audit rule to Greece.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Athens — national capital, dominant metro >3.1M
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: shipping/maritime services (world's largest merchant fleet by beneficial ownership), tourism, finance, government
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: Greek national identity centered on the capital; no separatism

autarky.rationale: Attica depends on imported water (Mornos/Evinos reservoirs, extended pipelines) and food from other regions, but leads the country on transport infrastructure (metro, port, airport) and healthcare capacity.

rationales.water: Attica depends on imported water (Mornos/Evinos reservoirs, extended pipelines) — the zone's characteristic capital-region weak point.
rationales.food: Food is imported from other regions; the capital is not agriculturally self-sufficient.
rationales.energy: Grid/import-dependent with no major regional generation asset.
rationales.transportation: Leads the country on transport infrastructure (metro, Piraeus port, airport).
rationales.hygiene_healthcare: Leads the country on healthcare capacity.

regions.name: Macedonia (Thessaloniki)
regions.identity_basis: GR SPLIT (mandated, supersedes v0.1.0's merged gr-thessaloniki-macedonia): Greek Macedonia, anchored by Thessaloniki (Greece's co-capital, former Ottoman/Sephardic-Jewish port city), now separated from Western Thrace's distinct Muslim-minority identity (see gr-thrace). Kentriki Makedonia (Thessaloniki core) and Dytiki Makedonia (Kozani lignite basin) share a Macedonian-Greek identity without Thrace's minority-demographic layer.
regions.population_note: Sum of Kentriki Makedonia (EL52, ~1.88M) and Dytiki Makedonia (EL53, ~0.26M), ELSTAT 2021 census; approximate.

pole.note: Overwhelmingly dominant; Kozani (West Macedonia) is a real but much smaller secondary industrial center.

reach.note: Thessaloniki functions as North Macedonia's historic outlet to the sea via the Vardar/Axios valley rail and road corridor (the shortest route from Skopje to a major port). The shared 'Macedonia' toponym remains politically sensitive even after the 2019 Prespa Agreement renamed the neighboring country North Macedonia; this reach entry describes an economic-geography fact (transit corridor, port hinterland), not a territorial or naming claim.

parliament.note: Greek perifereies are deconcentrated administrative units, not legislative parliaments.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Thessaloniki — metro >1M, Greece's second city and de facto northern capital
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: port trade, agro-processing, lignite-based power generation (West Macedonia)
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: strong regional identity; no separatism; now cleanly separated from Thrace's distinct minority-demographic layer

regions.nuts1_disagreement: Splits the former gr-thessaloniki-macedonia (EL51+EL52+EL53) along the EL51/EL52-53 boundary, isolating Western Thrace (Anatoliki Makedonia-Thraki, EL51) as its own unit — see gr-thrace.

autarky.rationale: Macedonian plain agriculture and Thessaloniki's port keep Food/Transportation strong; West Macedonia's lignite plants (Kozani/Ptolemaida) give the region unusually high domestic Energy generation capacity for Greece, even as national policy phases lignite out.

rationales.water: Macedonian-plain river access (Axios/Aliakmon) is adequate.
rationales.food: Macedonian plain agriculture keeps Food strong.
rationales.energy: West Macedonia's lignite plants (Kozani/Ptolemaida) give the region unusually high domestic Energy generation capacity for Greece, even as national policy phases lignite out.
rationales.transportation: Thessaloniki's port keeps Transportation strong.

regions.name: Thrace (Komotini-Alexandroupoli)
regions.identity_basis: GR SPLIT (mandated, supersedes v0.1.0's merged gr-thessaloniki-macedonia): Western Thrace carries Greece's officially-recognized Muslim minority (Turkish, Pomak, Roma), protected under the 1923 Treaty of Lausanne — a genuinely distinct demographic/religious layer from Macedonia's Greek-Orthodox majority, now given its own visible unit rather than a folded-in note.
regions.population_note: Anatoliki Makedonia kai Thraki (EL51), ELSTAT 2021 census.

pole.note: Alexandroupoli is the largest city and regional administrative capital, but Komotini (the historic Ottoman-era seat and largest Muslim-minority population center) and Xanthi are comparably significant — no single city organizes the whole area's identity.

parliament.note: Greek perifereies are deconcentrated administrative units, not legislative parliaments.

conflict_flags.description: Officially-recognized Muslim minority (Turkish, Pomak, Roma) protected under the 1923 Treaty of Lausanne, concentrated in the Xanthi-Komotini-Rodopi area — Greece's only legally recognized religious (not just ethnic) minority, a live and occasionally diplomatically sensitive Greek-Turkish bilateral issue.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: No single dominant hub — Alexandroupoli (~72k, admin capital), Komotini (~50k, minority center) and Xanthi (~55k) are comparable; a genuine weak point shared with gr-aegean-islands and bg-north-danube
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: tobacco, agriculture, lignite/energy transit, cross-border trade — thin diversification
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: a real, internationally-recognized minority-religious/ethnic layer (Lausanne Treaty) distinct from the rest of Greece; no separatism, but a live bilateral-diplomatic sensitivity with Turkey

regions.nuts1_disagreement: Splits the former gr-thessaloniki-macedonia (EL51+EL52+EL53) along the EL51/EL52-53 boundary, isolating this NUTS-2 unit exactly.
regions.lang_family: Hellenic (Greek) majority; Turkish, Pomak (Slavic-Muslim) and Roma minorities under Lausanne Treaty protection

autarky.rationale: A thinner agricultural and industrial base than Macedonia proper, reflecting the historically under-invested Greek-Turkish border position; tobacco farming and cross-border trade are its clearest economic assets.

rationales.water: Nestos/Evros river access is adequate.
rationales.food: Tobacco/agriculture base is real but thinner than the Macedonian plain.
rationales.energy: Lignite/energy transit infrastructure passes through but does not generate significant local capacity; import/grid-dependent.

sources: Treaty of Lausanne (1923), Section III on the Greek Muslim minority

regions.name: Crete
regions.identity_basis: Crete has a strong, historically-grounded distinct identity, having been an autonomous state (the Cretan State, 1898-1913) before uniting with Greece — a genuinely different case from the more diffuse Aegean Islands, kept deliberately separate rather than merged.
regions.population_note: Kriti (EL43), ELSTAT 2021 census.

pole.note: Heraklion dominates; Chania/Rethymno are real but clearly secondary.

parliament.note: Greek perifereies are deconcentrated administrative units, not legislative parliaments; Crete's historic 1898-1913 autonomous statehood is a cultural-identity fact, not a current legal status.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Heraklion — metro ~215k, Crete's dominant city
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: tourism, olive/wine agriculture, shipping
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: a strong, historically-grounded distinct identity (former Cretan State, 1898-1913) within Greece; no current separatism

autarky.rationale: Mediterranean water scarcity and heavy summer tourist-population swings strain Water; olive/wine agriculture is genuinely strong; the island imports nearly all fuel and manufactured goods.

rationales.water: Mediterranean water scarcity and heavy summer tourist-population swings strain Water.
rationales.food: Olive/wine agriculture is genuinely strong.
rationales.energy: The island imports nearly all fuel; no major domestic generation asset.

regions.name: Aegean Islands
regions.identity_basis: The North and South Aegean island groups (Lesvos, Chios, Samos; the Cyclades and Dodecanese including Rhodes) share a maritime, historically Genoese/Venetian/Ottoman-administered island culture distinct from mainland Greece, but are themselves a loose archipelago without one shared urban center.
regions.population_note: Sum of Voreio Aigaio (EL41, ~200k) + Notio Aigaio (EL42, ~310k), ELSTAT 2021 census; approximate.

pole.note: No dominant hub across the archipelago — Rhodes (Dodecanese) and Mytilene (North Aegean) anchor separate island groups.

parliament.note: Greek perifereies are deconcentrated administrative units, not legislative parliaments.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: No single dominant hub — Rhodes (~50k town) and Mytilene (~28k) are the largest, both far below this zone's other urban cores; FAILS this prong on any strict reading
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: tourism monoculture; fishing and small agriculture are marginal by comparison — FAILS the diversification prong
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: genuine shared maritime-island identity within Greece; no separatism

autarky.rationale: The zone's clearest case of a region failing the diversified-industry and single-urban-hub prongs of the inclusion test: near-total tourism dependence, imported water via tanker/desalination on several islands, imported fuel and virtually all manufactured goods. Retained as its own region only because Global Constraint #4's national-coverage requirement leaves no honest alternative home for ~510k islanders; kept deliberately separate from Crete (which does pass the test) rather than diluting Crete's strong case by merger.

rationales.water: Imported water via tanker/desalination on several islands — one of the dataset's lowest scores.
rationales.food: Near-total tourism dependence leaves little room for food self-sufficiency.
rationales.energy: Imported fuel; no significant domestic generation asset, one of the dataset's lowest scores.

regions.name: Peloponnese, Central Greece & Ionian Islands
regions.name_local: Πελοπόννησος, Στερεά Ελλάδα και Ιόνια Νησιά
regions.identity_basis: A mainland-plus-Ionian catch-all combining Epirus, Thessaly, the Ionian Islands, Western Greece, Central Greece (Sterea) and the Peloponnese. IONIAN ISLANDS VERDICT (explicit decision per draft_v0.1.2's coverage mandate): the Ionian Islands (EL62 — Corfu, Zakynthos, Kefalonia, Lefkada) are kept HERE, attached to the western/Epirus mainland side, rather than split into their own unit or attached to the Aegean archipelago. Reasoning: geographically the Ionian chain runs immediately off the Epirus/Western-Greece coast (Corfu faces Epirus, Kefalonia/Zakynthos face Achaia/Elis), with historic ferry/administrative links to the mainland opposite each island (not to the Aegean, which lies on the other side of the country); this is the 'northern/western mainland' attachment the brief's decision criterion names. The Ionian Islands' own Venetian-ruled (never Ottoman) history is a genuine distinguishing layer we note rather than erase by making a separate-unit case for them, since Aegean-style archipelago-wide urban/industry weakness (see gr-aegean-islands) does not apply as strongly here (Corfu town is a substantial, UNESCO-listed urban center) — a borderline call, stated honestly rather than silently resolved.
regions.population_note: Sum of Ipeiros (EL54, ~330k), Thessalia (EL61, ~680k), Ionia Nisia (EL62, ~205k), Dytiki Ellada (EL63, ~640k), Sterea Ellada (EL64, ~540k), Peloponnisos (EL65, ~560k), ELSTAT 2021 census; approximate.

pole.note: No city dominates the way Athens/Thessaloniki/Heraklion do for their regions; Patras is largest but Ioannina and Corfu are real, distinct sub-poles — honest reflection of this catch-all's weak identity case.

parliament.note: Greek perifereies are deconcentrated administrative units, not legislative parliaments.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Patras — metro ~215k, the largest single city, but no city here dominates the way Athens/Thessaloniki/Heraklion do for their regions; a genuinely weak fit
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: agriculture, tourism, port trade, light manufacturing — real but dispersed across six sub-areas rather than concentrated
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: the Peloponnese sub-area has strong distinct identity; Epirus, Thessaly and the Ionian Islands likewise each have real distinct character; the combined region as drawn has no single shared identity — retained for coverage, explicitly flagged as this zone's other borderline inclusion-test case alongside the Aegean Islands and Northern Bulgaria

regions.nuts1_disagreement: Real NUTS-1 groupings (EL6 'Kentriki Ellada' = Thessaly+Ionian+W.Greece+Sterea+Peloponnese) already merge five distinct sub-areas; we additionally fold in Epirus (EL54, part of NUTS-1 EL5 with Macedonia) because splitting it out alone would add a 24th zone-7 region for ~330k people with a thin urban hub (Ioannina, ~65k). This remains the single most defensible-but-uncomfortable merge in this file; the Ionian Islands' attachment here (rather than a standalone unit or Aegean-archipelago attachment) is the explicit new verdict for draft_v0.1.2.
regions.lang_family: Hellenic (Greek); Ionian Islands' Venetian-era Catholic minority heritage (small, historic)

autarky.rationale: Broad Mediterranean agricultural base (olives, citrus, cotton) supports Food; Patras port and moderate road network support middling Transportation; the region imports most manufactured clothing and much of its fuel.

rationales.water: Broad Mediterranean/Ionian coastal access is adequate but unremarkable.
rationales.food: Broad Mediterranean agricultural base (olives, citrus, cotton) supports Food.
rationales.energy: Grid/import-dependent; no major domestic generation asset.

regions.name: Cyprus
regions.identity_basis: Single-unit exception per Global Constraints; island nation, EU member since 2004, de facto divided since 1974 (Green Line). GEOMETRY VERDICT (checked, documented limitation rather than a fake boundary): NO clean north/south geometry source exists. (1) The committed GISCO NUTS2024 raw file carries only whole-island CY/CY0/CY00/CY000 codes (verified against pipeline/raw/NUTS_RG_20M_2024_4326.geojson — no sub-island feature exists). (2) A live geoBoundaries API check found CYP ADM1 has 6 units, but these are Cyprus's 6 pre-1974 historic districts (Nicosia, Limassol, Larnaca, Famagusta, Paphos, Kyrenia) — several of which (Nicosia, Famagusta) are THEMSELVES bisected by the 1974 ceasefire Green Line, so using them would misrepresent the actual de facto division rather than depict it, the opposite of the honesty this dataset otherwise insists on. DECISION: keep ONE region, add special_status (dashed rendering) and a strengthened conflict_flag documenting the split explicitly as a north/south-split-pending-geometry-source limitation, per the plan's own pre-authorized fallback.
regions.population_note: CY0, Statistical Service of Cyprus (CYSTAT) Census 2021, government-controlled area; approximate.

pole.note: Capital and largest city, itself bisected by the Green Line (a fact the special_status/dashed rendering should visually echo, per the app-wave legend).

parliament.name: House of Representatives (Vouli ton Antiprosopon)
parliament.note: Single-unit exception country: 'own parliament' here is Cyprus's own national parliament (government-controlled area only); the self-declared 'Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus' assembly is not internationally recognized (recognized only by Turkey) and is not modeled as a second parliament in this dataset.

conflict_flags.description: De facto division since the 1974 Turkish intervention: the Republic of Cyprus (EU member, government-controlled ~63% of the island, modeled here) vs. the self-declared, Turkey-only-recognized 'Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus' (~37%), separated by the UN-patrolled Green Line (itself bisecting Nicosia). NO CLEAN GEOMETRY SOURCE EXISTS for a north/south sub-division (see identity_basis for the documented 5-minute geometry check: GISCO whole-island-only; geoBoundaries CYP ADM1's 6 districts predate 1974 and are themselves split by the line). North/south split explicitly PENDING a better geometry source — a deliberate, stated limitation, not a silently-resolved one.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Nicosia — capital and largest city
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: financial services, shipping registry, tourism, real estate
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: EU member state; single-unit exception per Global Constraints

regions.lang_family: Hellenic (Greek Cypriot majority, government-controlled area); Turkish (Turkish Cypriot) in the de facto administered north, outside this dataset's population/economic figures

autarky.rationale: Mediterranean water scarcity is chronic and desalination-dependent; the island imports nearly all fuel and manufactured goods, but has strong healthcare capacity for its size.

rationales.water: Mediterranean water scarcity is chronic and desalination-dependent.
rationales.food: The island imports a significant share of its food; agriculture is real but limited by water scarcity.
rationales.energy: The island imports nearly all fuel; no significant domestic generation asset.

sources: Statistical Service of Cyprus (CYSTAT) — Population Census 2021
geoBoundaries CYP ADM1 metadata (checked 2026-07-05: 6 pre-1974 districts, not a north/south split)

regions.name: Malta
regions.identity_basis: Single-unit exception per Global Constraints; small island nation, EU member since 2004.
regions.population_note: Malta (MT00), National Statistics Office Malta 2023 estimate.

pole.note: Small, dense island-state; Valletta is the formal capital though the urban conurbation is largely continuous.

parliament.name: House of Representatives of Malta
parliament.note: Single-unit exception country: 'own parliament' here is Malta's own national parliament.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Valletta/greater urban area — the whole main island functions as one dense conurbation
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: financial services, tourism, iGaming, shipping registry
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: EU member state; single-unit exception per Global Constraints

autarky.rationale: Malta has essentially no domestic freshwater or energy resources (desalination and imported fuel/interconnector power dominate); dense urban fabric and EU-funded healthcare give it comparatively strong Shelter and Hygiene & Healthcare for its size.

rationales.water: Essentially no domestic freshwater resources; desalination dominates.
rationales.food: Very limited arable land; the island imports most food.
rationales.energy: Essentially no domestic energy resources; imported fuel and the Malta-Sicily interconnector dominate.

regions.name: Belgrade & Central Serbia
regions.name_local: Београд и централна Србија / Beograd i centralna Srbija
regions.identity_basis: Belgrade as national capital overwhelmingly dominates central Serbia (Šumadija and western/southern Serbia) economically, politically and culturally.
regions.population_note: Sum of Beogradski region and Region Šumadije i Zapadne Srbije + Region Južne i Istočne Srbije, RZS (Statistical Office of Serbia) 2023 estimate.
