pole.note: Overwhelmingly dominant national capital.

parliament.note: Central Serbia has no separate autonomous assembly (unlike Vojvodina); ordinary Serbian administrative regions, per the explicit RS audit rule.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Belgrade — national capital, dominant metro >1.7M
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: government/finance, automotive (Fiat/Stellantis Kragujevac), lignite power, IT
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: Serbian national identity centered on the capital; no separatism

autarky.rationale: The Kolubara/Kostolac lignite basins make this region (and Serbia generally) unusually energy self-sufficient for the zone, though coal-heavy and environmentally costly — a genuinely mid rather than high score given air-quality and long-term supply tradeoffs; Belgrade's infrastructure lifts Transportation and Hygiene & Healthcare above the regional baseline.

rationales.water: Danube/Sava/Morava river-basin access is abundant.
rationales.food: Šumadija/central-Serbia agriculture supports a solid food score.
rationales.energy: The Kolubara/Kostolac lignite basins make this region (and Serbia generally) unusually energy self-sufficient for the zone, though coal-heavy and environmentally costly.
rationales.transportation: Belgrade's infrastructure lifts Transportation above the regional baseline.

sources: Statistical Office of the Republic of Serbia (RZS) 2023

regions.name: Vojvodina (Novi Sad)
regions.identity_basis: Vojvodina's Habsburg-era autonomous heritage and its present-day constitutionally-recognized Autonomous Province status (with its own Assembly) set it clearly apart from central Serbia; a genuinely multi-ethnic province (Hungarian, Slovak, Croatian, Rusyn and Romanian minorities alongside a Serb majority).
regions.population_note: Autonomna Pokrajina Vojvodina (RS12 correspondence), RZS 2023 estimate.

pole.note: Novi Sad dominates as the provincial capital; Subotica (Hungarian-minority center) is a real but clearly secondary city.

parliament.name: Assembly of the Autonomous Province of Vojvodina (Skupština APV)
parliament.note: Real, constitutionally-recognized autonomous provincial assembly under the Serbian Constitution — the clearest 'has_own: true' case in this file alongside the BA entities.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Novi Sad — metro ~380k, Vojvodina's capital and second city of Serbia
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: Pannonian grain belt agriculture, food processing, petrochemicals, growing IT sector
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: genuine Habsburg-era autonomous heritage and present constitutional Autonomous Province status; multi-ethnic composition (Hungarian/Slovak/Croatian/Rusyn/Romanian minorities); no separatism, organic historically-grown distinctness (contrasted in v0.1.0's push-back note with post-conflict administrative partitions like BA's entities)

regions.lang_family: South Slavic (Serbian) majority; Hungarian, Slovak, Rusyn, Croatian and Romanian minorities with co-official status in parts of the province

autarky.rationale: The Pannonian plain is Serbia's (and one of Europe's) most productive grain belts, giving Food the zone's near-top score; Novi Sad's river/rail position supports Transportation, but Vojvodina lacks central Serbia's coal-power base, capping Energy.

rationales.water: The Danube-Tisza-Danube canal system and Pannonian plain give abundant water access.
rationales.food: The Pannonian plain is Serbia's (and one of Europe's) most productive grain belts, giving Food the zone's near-top score.
rationales.energy: Vojvodina lacks central Serbia's coal-power base, capping Energy despite Pančevo's petrochemical processing.
rationales.transportation: Novi Sad's river/rail position supports Transportation.

sources: Statistical Office of the Republic of Serbia (RZS) 2023
Constitution of the Republic of Serbia, Art. 182-183 on Vojvodina's autonomy

regions.name: Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina
regions.identity_basis: SUPERSEDES v0.1.0's single-region verdict: Bosnia's three Dayton Agreement (1995) entities are now modeled as three separate units, each with its own real constitutional parliament (the parliament rule mandates this). The Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina — itself a federation of 10 cantons — is the more urbanized, Bosniak-Croat-majority entity, anchored by Sarajevo (the shared, though contested, national capital) and including Mostar (Croat-Bosniak divided city) and the Tuzla/Zenica industrial belt.
regions.population_note: Agency for Statistics of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Census 2013 (last full census; contested — see ba-republika-srpska for the same caveat).

pole.note: The Federation is itself a federation of 10 cantons; Sarajevo dominates but Mostar and Tuzla are real, distinct secondary poles, an honest polycentric case.

parliament.name: Parliament of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina
parliament.note: Real constitutional legislature (Dayton Agreement, 1995); one of the two entity-level parliaments alongside Republika Srpska's National Assembly, plus Brčko District's Assembly — the clearest 3-way parliament-rule case in this dataset.

conflict_flags.description: Internal entity boundaries from the 1995 Dayton Peace Agreement. Now modeled as three separate cultural units (ba-federation-bih, ba-republika-srpska, ba-brcko-district) rather than one region with an overlay flag, per the parliament rule (each entity has a real constitutional legislature) — SUPERSEDES v0.1.0's single-unit-with-flag treatment, which itself argued the Dayton partition was 'not organic regionalism'. That argument is preserved in the zone notes as background even though the mandate has changed: the three units exist because of real, current constitutional government, independent of whether the original 1995 partition was organic.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Sarajevo — metro ~550k, national and entity capital, historic Ottoman-then-Austro-Hungarian crossroads city
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: steel/metals (Zenica), IT/services (Sarajevo), tourism, agriculture
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: the Federation exists as a constitutional entity within the sovereign state of Bosnia and Herzegovina; no separatism at the Federation level (unlike some Republika Srpska political rhetoric — see that record)

regions.nuts1_disagreement: Uses the SR2024 statistical-regions code BA01, which resolves directly against the committed GISCO raw geometry file (pipeline/raw/NUTS_RG_20M_2024_4326.geojson) — NO geoBoundaries/ADM1 workaround is needed; the code and its geometry are already present in the same source used for the rest of this dataset.
regions.lang_family: South Slavic (Bosnian/Croatian, mutually intelligible with Serbian)

autarky.rationale: Neretva-basin hydropower and river resources give a real domestic energy base; mountainous terrain and post-war infrastructure gaps keep Transportation modest; Sarajevo's university-hospital complex supports healthcare relative to the rest of the entity.

rationales.water: Neretva/Bosna river basins give solid freshwater access.
rationales.food: Adequate, unremarkable agriculture; imports supplement domestic production.
rationales.energy: Hydroelectric capacity (Neretva basin) gives a genuine domestic generation base, though smaller than Republika Srpska's Drina/Vrbas hydro assets.

sources: Agency for Statistics of Bosnia and Herzegovina — Census 2013 (last full census; contested)
Dayton Peace Agreement (1995), Annex 4 (Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina)

regions.name: Republika Srpska
regions.identity_basis: SUPERSEDES v0.1.0's single-region verdict: Republika Srpska, the Serb-majority Dayton entity, has its own real constitutional National Assembly, president, and a high degree of governmental autonomy within Bosnia and Herzegovina (including periodic secessionist political rhetoric from entity leadership, though no legal secession has occurred) — the strongest real 'has_own parliament' case in this dataset alongside Vojvodina.
regions.population_note: Agency for Statistics of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Census 2013 (last full census; contested between entities over methodology and diaspora counting).

pole.note: Banja Luka dominates as the entity's de facto administrative capital.

parliament.name: National Assembly of Republika Srpska
parliament.note: Real constitutional legislature (Dayton Agreement, 1995) with an unusually high degree of practical autonomy, including its own president, government and periodic political rhetoric about further autonomy or secession (not currently legally enacted).

conflict_flags.description: Republika Srpska's entity-level leadership has periodically floated further autonomy or secession referenda (most prominently under President Milorad Dodik); no such move has legal effect under Bosnia's constitution or international law, and Republika Srpska remains a constituent entity of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Flagged as a live political fact distinct from the more settled Vojvodina/Federation cases.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Banja Luka — metro ~200k, entity's largest city and de facto capital
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: hydropower, timber, agriculture, light manufacturing
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: constitutionally a Bosnian entity, though with the dataset's most active autonomy/secession-adjacent political rhetoric — the honest edge case for the inclusion test's 'dependent, not seeking independence' criterion, alongside ro-szekely-land

regions.nuts1_disagreement: Uses the SR2024 statistical-regions code BA02, which resolves directly against the committed GISCO raw geometry file — no pipeline coordination or geoBoundaries workaround needed.

autarky.rationale: Extensive hydroelectric capacity (Drina, Vrbas basins) makes this entity a genuinely decent domestic energy producer and a regional electricity exporter, unusual for the zone; mountainous terrain and post-war infrastructure gaps keep Transportation low.

rationales.water: Drina/Vrbas river basins give strong freshwater access.
rationales.food: Adequate agriculture, comparable to the Federation.
rationales.energy: Extensive hydroelectric capacity (Drina, Vrbas basins) makes this entity a genuinely decent domestic energy producer and a regional electricity exporter, unusual for the zone.

sources: Agency for Statistics of Bosnia and Herzegovina — Census 2013 (last full census; contested)

regions.name: Brčko District
regions.identity_basis: SUPERSEDES v0.1.0's single-region verdict: Brčko District is a self-governing administrative unit under international (2000 arbitration) supervision, belonging to neither entity — jointly held by both under a condominium arrangement — with its own Assembly. The smallest of Bosnia's three parliament-rule units, included as its own unit precisely because the parliament rule does not carve out exceptions for size.
regions.population_note: Brčko District Statistics Office / Agency for Statistics of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Census 2013 (last full census; contested).

pole.note: Brčko town is the district's only urban center; the whole district is roughly town-sized.

parliament.name: Brčko District Assembly (Skupština Brčko distrikta)
parliament.note: Real self-governing assembly established by the 1999/2000 Brčko Arbitration Award, held jointly by both entities under international supervision — a unique third case alongside the Federation and Republika Srpska parliaments.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Brčko — the district's only town, ~40k; small by this dataset's usual standards but a genuine, distinct self-governing unit
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: river-port logistics on the Sava, agriculture, modest cross-border trade with Croatia
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: self-governing under international arbitration, held jointly by both Bosnian entities rather than belonging to either — no separatism, a genuine condominium arrangement

regions.nuts1_disagreement: Uses the SR2024 statistical-regions code BA03, which resolves directly against the committed GISCO raw geometry file — no pipeline coordination or geoBoundaries workaround needed, despite the district's small size and unusual legal status.
regions.lang_family: South Slavic (mixed Bosnian/Croatian/Serbian population, roughly equal thirds post-war)

autarky.rationale: A small river-port district with modest agriculture and logistics; too small for major domestic energy generation, and healthcare/shelter infrastructure is thinner than in either entity's larger cities.

rationales.water: Sava river access is adequate.
rationales.food: Small-scale agriculture; the smallest and most rural of the three BA units.
rationales.energy: No domestic generation asset; import/grid-dependent via both entities' grids.

sources: Agency for Statistics of Bosnia and Herzegovina — Census 2013 (last full census; contested)
Brčko Final Award (1999) and Supplemental Award (2000)

regions.name: Montenegro
regions.identity_basis: Single-unit exception per Global Constraints; small independent nation-state (independence 2006).
regions.population_note: MONSTAT (Statistical Office of Montenegro) 2023 estimate.

pole.note: Overwhelmingly dominant national capital; the Adriatic coast (Kotor, Budva) is a real tourism-economic secondary pole but not a population/administrative one.

parliament.name: Parliament of Montenegro (Skupština Crne Gore)
parliament.note: Single-unit exception country: 'own parliament' here is Montenegro's own national parliament.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Podgorica — capital and largest city
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: tourism, aluminum, hydro, maritime shipping
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: independent sovereign state; single-unit exception per Global Constraints

autarky.rationale: Mountainous terrain gives good freshwater and hydro capacity; coastal tourism dominates the economy over food self-sufficiency; road/rail connectivity through the Dinaric mountains remains genuinely limited.

rationales.water: Mountainous terrain gives good freshwater and hydro capacity.
rationales.food: Coastal tourism dominates the economy over food self-sufficiency; agriculture is real but limited.
rationales.energy: Hydro capacity is genuine, though the aluminum smelter's historic demand strains the domestic grid.

regions.name: North Macedonia
regions.identity_basis: Single-unit exception per Global Constraints; independent nation-state, renamed from 'Macedonia' to 'North Macedonia' under the 2018 Prespa Agreement with Greece.
regions.population_note: State Statistical Office of North Macedonia 2023 estimate.

pole.note: Overwhelmingly dominant national capital.

reach.note: See gr-macedonia's reciprocal reach entry: North Macedonia's historic economic outlet to the sea runs via Thessaloniki port and the Vardar/Axios corridor, an economic-geography fact independent of the two countries' post-Prespa-Agreement naming settlement.

parliament.name: Assembly of the Republic of North Macedonia (Sobranie)
parliament.note: Single-unit exception country: 'own parliament' here is North Macedonia's own national parliament.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Skopje — capital and largest city
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: textiles, agriculture, automotive supply, tourism
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: independent sovereign state; single-unit exception per Global Constraints; a real Albanian-minority regional layer in the west (Tetovo) noted but not split per the exception list

autarky.rationale: Pelagonia-plain agriculture supports Food; a genuine (if low-margin) textile industry gives Clothing a real domestic base, comparable to Plovdiv/Thrace in this zone; landlocked geography and mountainous terrain constrain Transportation.

rationales.water: Vardar river-basin access is adequate.
rationales.food: Pelagonia-plain agriculture supports Food.
rationales.energy: Coal/hydro mix, moderate; landlocked geography limits import flexibility somewhat.
rationales.clothing: A genuine, if low-margin, textile industry gives Clothing a real domestic base.

sources: State Statistical Office of North Macedonia 2023

regions.name: Albania
regions.identity_basis: Single-unit exception per Global Constraints; independent nation-state.
regions.population_note: INSTAT (Albanian Institute of Statistics) 2023 estimate.

pole.note: Overwhelmingly dominant national capital; Durrës (main port) is a real but clearly secondary city.

parliament.name: Assembly of Albania (Kuvendi)
parliament.note: Single-unit exception country: 'own parliament' here is Albania's own national parliament.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Tirana — capital and largest city
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: hydropower, tourism, agriculture, contract textiles/footwear manufacturing
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: independent sovereign state; single-unit exception per Global Constraints

autarky.rationale: Albania is one of Europe's most hydro-dependent power systems and a net electricity exporter in wet years (Drin river cascade), giving Energy a genuinely high score for the zone; chronic under-investment in housing stock and healthcare outside Tirana, plus mountainous terrain, keep Shelter, Transportation and Hygiene & Healthcare low.

rationales.water: Abundant Alpine/Dinaric freshwater resources feed the Drin river cascade.
rationales.food: Agriculture is real though under-modernized; adequate rather than exceptional.
rationales.energy: Albania is one of Europe's most hydro-dependent power systems and a net electricity exporter in wet years (Drin river cascade), giving Energy a genuinely high score for the zone.

regions.name: Kosovo
regions.identity_basis: Single-unit exception per Global Constraints; partially-recognized independent state (declared 2008, recognized by ~100 UN members, not by Serbia/Russia/China/5 EU states). Mitrovica's Serb-majority north is a live, distinct minority-conflict layer within the single-unit treatment.
regions.population_note: Kosovo Agency of Statistics 2023 estimate.

pole.note: Overwhelmingly dominant national capital.

parliament.name: Assembly of Kosovo (Kuvendi i Kosovës)
parliament.note: Single-unit exception country: 'own parliament' here is Kosovo's own (partially-recognized) national parliament.

conflict_flags.description: Serb-majority North Mitrovica and adjacent municipalities remain a live flashpoint (parallel Serbian-backed institutions, periodic unrest, EU/NATO-mediated normalization talks); a distinct minority-conflict layer within the single-unit treatment, not modeled as a separate geometry given Kosovo's own single-unit exception status.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Pristina — capital and largest city
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: lignite power, legacy mining (Trepča), textiles/apparel export, diaspora remittances
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: partially-recognized independent state; single-unit exception per Global Constraints; the North Mitrovica Serb-minority layer is a live, internationally-mediated issue noted via conflict_flag rather than a redrawn boundary

regions.lang_family: Albanian majority; Serbian minority concentrated in North Mitrovica

autarky.rationale: The Kosovo A/B lignite plants near Pristina make Kosovo highly energy self-sufficient in raw generation terms (if environmentally very costly and technically unreliable); a real textile/apparel export sector gives Clothing a workable score; landlocked, mountainous terrain and a housing stock strained by post-war reconstruction and heavy return-migration keep Shelter and Transportation low.

rationales.water: Adequate but strained by aging Yugoslav-era infrastructure.
rationales.food: Agriculture is real but under-modernized; moderate self-sufficiency.
rationales.energy: The Kosovo A/B lignite plants near Pristina make Kosovo highly energy self-sufficient in raw generation terms, if environmentally very costly and technically unreliable.

regions.name: Kyiv
regions.identity_basis: Capital region; seat of Ukrainian statehood since Kyivan Rus'; distinct administrative status as a city of national significance separate from surrounding Kyiv Oblast.
regions.population_note: Sum of Kyiv city (~2.95M) and Kyiv Oblast (~1.79M), 2021 Ukrstat estimates. Wartime displacement (2022- ) reduced city population by an estimated 20-25% at the invasion's peak with partial return since, so current figures carry substantial uncertainty.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Kyiv, metro >3M, national political/cultural/media capital
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: IT services, finance, food processing, logistics, public administration
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: capital-region identity fully integrated into Ukrainian statehood, no separatism

regions.nuts1_disagreement: Ukraine has no official EU-style NUTS-1; the SR2024 substitute groups Kyiv city and Kyiv Oblast under separate level-2 codes (UAC3, UAC1) within Macroregion C (UAC) with no other oblasts, so this region matches the SR macroregion boundary exactly.

autarky.rationale: Capital and national transport/rail hub with strong administrative/service economy; energy repeatedly targeted by missile strikes since 2022, reducing that score; relies on surrounding oblasts for food rather than being a major agricultural producer itself.

rationales.water: Dnipro reservoirs cascade through the region; supply ample though quality-stressed.
rationales.food: Kyiv oblast chernozem is productive, but the metro is a net consumer.
rationales.energy: Hosts grid-control hub and thermal plants, yet the capital depends on national generation repeatedly damaged by strikes.

sources: State Statistics Service of Ukraine (Ukrstat), 2021 population estimates
Kyiv City State Administration statistical yearbook

pole.note: Capital monopole: Kyiv city plus oblast orient entirely on the capital.

reach.note: Kyiv's political, media and wartime-coordination reach spans the whole state; its labour catchment covers several neighbouring oblasts.

parliament.note: No regional legislature; oblast councils (oblasna rada) are organs of local self-government under Ukraine's unitary constitution, not parliaments.

regions.name: Lviv / Galicia
regions.identity_basis: Historic Eastern Galicia (Austro-Hungarian Empire, then interwar Poland until 1939) plus Bukovina (Chernivtsi; Austro-Hungarian/Romanian until 1940); strong Ukrainian Greek Catholic identity, distinct dialect and pro-European civic culture. Grouped as a broader 'Western Ukraine' region for zone-coverage reasons - Bukovina's distinct Austro-Romanian heritage differs from Galicia proper and is bundled here rather than modelled as a separate region, given the zone's target region count (caveat stated explicitly, see zone notes).
regions.population_note: Sum of 2021 Ukrstat oblast estimates for Lviv, Ivano-Frankivsk, Ternopil, and Chernivtsi. This region absorbed large numbers of internally displaced persons from eastern/southern Ukraine after 2022, so current population likely exceeds this pre-war baseline.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Lviv, metro ~1.7M (city+region), major cultural/university/tech centre
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: IT services, furniture/wood, tourism, food processing
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: strong regional Galician identity within Ukraine; pro-Ukrainian, no separatism

regions.nuts1_disagreement: SR2024 places these oblasts in Macroregion 07 (UA7) with no additional oblasts beyond the four grouped here, so the region matches the SR macroregion; however it merges two historically distinct entities (Galicia proper: Lviv/Ivano-Frankivsk/Ternopil, vs Bukovina: Chernivtsi) for coverage reasons - flagged explicitly rather than silently assumed identical.

autarky.rationale: Western Ukraine largely spared direct ground war; solid agriculture though less black-soil than the central steppe; light industry (furniture, textiles, IT); still dependent on the national grid for energy despite some EU interconnection.

rationales.water: Carpathian foothill catchments give reliable supply.
rationales.food: Mixed farming solid though less fertile than the chernozem belt.
rationales.energy: Western grid interconnection to the EU (ENTSO-E) is a strategic asset; generation itself modest.

sources: Magocsi, P.R. - Historical Atlas of Central Europe (Galicia/Bukovina boundaries)

pole.note: Lviv is Galicia's uncontested cultural-economic capital.

reach.note: Lviv functions as the gateway for the Polish/Slovak/Hungarian borderlands and for the large Ukrainian diaspora; since 2022 it is also the primary safe-haven hub and westward logistics corridor.

parliament.note: No regional legislature; oblast councils (oblasna rada) are organs of local self-government under Ukraine's unitary constitution, not parliaments.

conflict_flags.description: Concentrated ethnic Hungarian minority (~100,000-150,000, plurality in Berehove/Berehovo district) and a distinct Rusyn identity movement (recognised as a separate ethnicity by Slovakia, Serbia, and others; treated as a Ukrainian sub-ethnos, not a nationality, under Ukrainian law) create a genuine cross-border/identity layer distinct from the oblast's Ukrainian majority.

regions.name: Zakarpattia
regions.identity_basis: Former Subcarpathian Rus', part of Hungary/Czechoslovakia until 1945; distinct Rusyn ethnolinguistic identity (recognised as a separate nationality by several neighbouring states but classified as a Ukrainian sub-group domestically) and a concentrated ethnic Hungarian minority (plurality in Berehove district); isolated west of the Carpathian ridge from the rest of Ukraine.
regions.population_note: 2021 Ukrstat oblast estimate. The least war-disrupted Ukrainian oblast and a net recipient of internally displaced persons since 2022, so current population is likely higher.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Uzhhorod, regional administrative/cultural centre, ~115k
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: furniture, viticulture/fruit growing, tourism, cross-border light manufacturing
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: distinct Rusyn/Hungarian-minority layered identity, dependent within Ukraine, no separatist movement despite historical border changes

regions.nuts1_disagreement: SR2024 Macroregion 07 (UA7) groups Zakarpattia with Ivano-Frankivsk/Ternopil/Chernivtsi; split out here as its own region given its markedly distinct Subcarpathian-Rusyn/Hungarian-minority identity, Carpathian geographic isolation, and separate historical trajectory (Hungary/Czechoslovakia vs Polish Galicia).

autarky.rationale: Mountainous region with abundant mineral-water sources and moderate fruit/viticulture agriculture but limited arable land; Carpathian isolation reduces transport connectivity; the least war-affected Ukrainian oblast, functioning partly as an internal-refugee haven.

rationales.water: Carpathian headwaters (Tysa basin) give abundant water.
rationales.food: Mountain terrain limits arable; lowland strip vineyards/orchards only.
rationales.energy: Small hydro plus the EU grid interconnect; largely import-dependent.

sources: Council of Europe minority-rights reporting on Hungarian/Rusyn populations in Zakarpattia
Magocsi, P.R. - history of Subcarpathian Rus'

pole.note: Uzhhorod anchors the oblast; Mukachevo is a close second in a small region.

parliament.note: No regional legislature; oblast councils (oblasna rada) are organs of local self-government under Ukraine's unitary constitution, not parliaments.

conflict_flags.description: Parts of Kherson Oblast east of the Dnipro river remain under Russian occupation since 2022 with an active front line along the river; the Kakhovka dam destruction (June 2023) caused catastrophic flooding and destroyed regional irrigation infrastructure.

regions.name: Odesa / Southern Ukraine
regions.identity_basis: Black Sea maritime/port identity centred on multi-ethnic, historically cosmopolitan Odesa (founded under Catherine II; Greek/Jewish/Italian/multi-ethnic heritage). Mykolaiv and Kherson share the Black Sea steppe coastal economy and are grouped with Odesa as the dominant regional hub, per the zone-8 mandate that Odesa be modelled as its own distinct region.
regions.population_note: Sum of 2021 Ukrstat oblast estimates (Odesa, Mykolaiv, Kherson). Kherson Oblast figures are highly uncertain post-2022 given partial Russian occupation (2022-2023), the November 2022 liberation of Kherson city, and the June 2023 Kakhovka dam destruction, which displaced tens of thousands from the flood zone.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Odesa, metro ~1M, Ukraine's principal Black Sea port and a UNESCO World Heritage historic centre
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: port logistics, grain export, shipbuilding, agriculture, tourism
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: cosmopolitan Black Sea regional identity within Ukraine, no separatism despite historical 'Novorossiya' Russian irredentist claims (rejected locally)

regions.nuts1_disagreement: SR2024 Macroregion 04 (UA4) groups Odesa, Mykolaiv, Kherson AND Crimea/Sevastopol together; this region excludes Crimea/Sevastopol, modelled separately (ua-crimea) given their distinct occupied status since 2014, eight years before Kherson's occupation began.

autarky.rationale: Prime agricultural/grain-export region (Odesa port) drives the food score, but war has severely damaged port infrastructure, Kherson front-line fighting has devastated shelter, and the Kakhovka dam destruction (2023) crippled regional irrigation/hydropower.

rationales.water: Dnister/Dnipro lowland abstraction; Kherson canal systems war-damaged (Kakhovka dam destruction).
rationales.food: Steppe grain and sunflower belt plus the grain-export ports.
rationales.energy: Thermal and wind assets degraded by strikes; net importer.

sources: UN OCHA Ukraine situation reports on Kherson flood/occupation impacts

pole.note: Odesa dominates the Black Sea littoral; Mykolaiv and Kherson are secondary.

parliament.note: No regional legislature; oblast councils (oblasna rada) are organs of local self-government under Ukraine's unitary constitution, not parliaments.

regions.name: Kharkiv / Slobozhanshchyna
regions.identity_basis: Historic Sloboda Ukraine (Slobozhanshchyna), settled by Cossack frontier militia in the 17th century; Kharkiv served as Ukraine's first Soviet-era capital (1919-1934) and remains a major scientific/university/industrial centre with a mixed Ukrainian-Russian-speaking urban culture.
regions.population_note: Sum of 2021 Ukrstat oblast estimates (Kharkiv, Sumy). Kharkiv city and oblast experienced the heaviest population outflow of any major Ukrainian region after February 2022 due to sustained shelling near the Russian border, with only partial return as of 2024-25.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Kharkiv, pre-war metro ~2M, Ukraine's second city, major university/research/industrial centre
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: machine building, aerospace components, research institutes, agriculture
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: Sloboda Ukrainian regional identity within Ukraine, historically Russian-speaking but strongly pro-Ukrainian since 2022, no separatism

regions.nuts1_disagreement: SR2024 Macroregion A (UAA) groups Kharkiv, Sumy AND Chernihiv together; Chernihiv is modelled here instead within the Central-Podillia catch-all region given its Polissia-woodland geography and weaker functional ties to Kharkiv's Sloboda-steppe identity.

autarky.rationale: Kharkiv city repeatedly shelled/near the front since 2022 with heavy infrastructure damage; surrounding Sloboda farmland remains productive; the energy grid is frequently targeted, causing recurring blackouts.

rationales.water: Siverskyi Donets basin adequate in peacetime; infrastructure repeatedly struck.
rationales.food: Productive chernozem despite front-line proximity.
rationales.energy: Generation and grid systematically targeted since 2022; severe deficit.

sources: Kharkiv Regional Military Administration humanitarian reports

pole.note: Kharkiv, Ukraine's second city, entirely dominates Slobozhanshchyna.

parliament.note: No regional legislature; oblast councils (oblasna rada) are organs of local self-government under Ukraine's unitary constitution, not parliaments.

conflict_flags.description: Approximately 70-80% of Donetsk Oblast's pre-war territory, including the regional capital Donetsk city, Mariupol, and Horlivka, has been under Russian occupation since 2014 (partial) and April-May 2022 (Mariupol), with an active front line running through the remainder; Ukrainian government administration relocated to Kramatorsk.

regions.name: Donetsk
regions.identity_basis: Historic Donbas coal-and-steel industrial basin, heavily Russified under Soviet industrialisation; Ukrainian regional administration relocated from occupied Donetsk city to Kramatorsk after 2014; distinct industrial-proletarian identity now overlaid by active war and large-scale Russian occupation since 2014 (partial) and 2022 (major expansion).
regions.population_note: 2021 Ukrstat oblast estimate for the whole oblast as of that date. By 2024-25 the government-controlled portion of Donetsk Oblast has lost the large majority of its pre-war population to displacement, and a substantial share of the oblast (including Donetsk city, Mariupol, and most industrial areas) is under Russian occupation with population figures unverifiable from Ukrainian sources - treat this figure as a pre-war ceiling, not a current count.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Kramatorsk (relocated oblast administrative seat) / historic hub Donetsk city (occupied); pre-war conurbation >2M
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: coal, steel, heavy machinery (pre-war baseline; severely war-degraded)
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: distinct Donbas industrial identity within Ukraine; the Russian-backed separatist project since 2014 is explicitly rejected as illegitimate by the Ukrainian state and the vast majority of the international community - included here as Ukrainian territory per international law, with occupation flagged, not as an endorsement of separatist claims

regions.nuts1_disagreement: SR2024 Macroregion 02 (UA2) groups Donetsk with Luhansk; modelled as two separate regions here per the zone-8 mandate that Donetsk and Luhansk each be distinct, reflecting their historically separate oblast administrations despite a shared Donbas identity.

autarky.rationale: Active war zone with large portions occupied/destroyed since 2014/2022; heavy industry (coal/steel) devastated; infrastructure severely war-degraded across every dimension, most acutely shelter and energy.

rationales.water: Siverskyi Donets canal largely destroyed; acute wartime shortage.
rationales.food: Steppe farmland heavily mined and depopulated.
rationales.energy: Coal-industrial base wrecked or under occupation.

sources: UN OCHA/UNHCR Ukraine displacement reporting for Donetsk Oblast
Kyiv School of Economics war-damage assessments

pole.note: Donetsk city was the agglomeration core; Mariupol was the second pole before its 2022 destruction.

parliament.note: No regional legislature; oblast councils (oblasna rada) are organs of local self-government under Ukraine's unitary constitution, not parliaments.

conflict_flags.description: Nearly the entire pre-war territory of Luhansk Oblast, including the former administrative centre Luhansk city and the wartime-relocated seat Sievierodonetsk, has been under Russian or Russian-backed separatist control since 2014 (partial) and 2022 (near-total); Ukrainian government control is limited to small border areas.

regions.name: Luhansk
regions.identity_basis: Eastern Donbas coal-mining oblast; the vast majority of Luhansk Oblast has been under Russian/separatist occupation since 2014, expanding to near-total occupation after 2022; shares a Donbas industrial-Russified identity with Donetsk but is administered as a historically separate oblast.
regions.population_note: 2021 Ukrstat oblast estimate as a pre-war ceiling. The oblast is now almost entirely under Russian occupation and current population is unverifiable from Ukrainian government sources; treat with high uncertainty.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Luhansk city (occupied) / Sievierodonetsk (relocated seat, occupied since June 2022)
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: coal mining, chemical industry (pre-war baseline, severely war-degraded)
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: Donbas industrial identity within Ukraine; Russian-backed separatist claims since 2014 rejected as illegitimate under international law - included as Ukrainian territory with occupation flagged

regions.nuts1_disagreement: SR2024 Macroregion 02 (UA2) groups Luhansk with Donetsk; modelled separately per the zone-8 mandate for distinct Donetsk/Luhansk regions.

autarky.rationale: Comparable war devastation to Donetsk: near-total occupation since 2014/2022, collapsed coal/chemical industry, and severely degraded infrastructure across every autarky dimension.

rationales.water: Donets tributaries adequate physically; systems war-damaged.
rationales.food: Steppe farming disrupted by full occupation.
rationales.energy: Coal-based generation under occupation; effectively severed from Ukraine's grid.

sources: OSCE Special Monitoring Mission to Ukraine archival reporting (2014-2022)

pole.note: Luhansk city dominates; Sievierodonetsk agglomeration destroyed/occupied since 2022.

parliament.note: No regional legislature; oblast councils (oblasna rada) are organs of local self-government under Ukraine's unitary constitution, not parliaments.

conflict_flags.description: The Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant, Europe's largest, and roughly the eastern half of Zaporizhzhia Oblast (including Melitopol and Berdiansk) have been under Russian occupation since 2022, with the plant offline and repeatedly at risk amid front-line fighting; flag limited to the occupied/frontline districts of the oblast, distinct from unoccupied Dnipropetrovsk.

regions.name: Dnipro / Zaporizhzhia
regions.identity_basis: Central-eastern industrial heartland along the lower Dnipro; historic Zaporozhian Sich free-steppe territory (origin of the Zaporizhzhia name) later colonised as the empire's 'New Russia' frontier; major heavy-industry/aerospace/metallurgy base (Dnipro rocket engines, Kryvyi Rih iron-ore basin, Zaporizhzhia steel and nuclear power). Kirovohrad oblast (Kropyvnytskyi) is re-homed here from the former central catch-all: its steppe settlement history is Zaporozhian-frontier rather than Hetmanate-regimental, and its economy ties into the Kryvyi Rih mining basin that straddles the oblast line.
key_industries: nuclear power (Zaporizhzhia NPP, currently Russian-occupied and offline)
regions.population_note: Sum of 2021 Ukrstat oblast estimates (Dnipropetrovsk, Zaporizhzhia, Kirovohrad ~0.90M). Zaporizhzhia city and the government-controlled western part of that oblast lie near an active front line since 2022, causing significant displacement not yet reflected in this baseline.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Dnipro, metro >1.5M, major industrial/aerospace centre
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: steel, iron ore, aerospace/rocketry, nuclear power, machine building
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: distinct Cossack-heritage industrial regional identity within Ukraine, no separatism in government-controlled areas

regions.nuts1_disagreement: SR2024 Macroregion B (UAB) groups Dnipropetrovsk and Zaporizhzhia; Kirovohrad (UA91, SR macroregion UA9) is added here on Zaporozhian-steppe historical and Kryvyi-Rih economic grounds - the explicit re-homing decision required by draft-v0.1.2 when the central catch-all was dissolved.

autarky.rationale: Major industrial base (steel, iron ore, aerospace, nuclear) and solid agriculture, but Zaporizhzhia city's proximity to the front and the occupied/offline Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant - a major national energy loss - depress shelter and energy scores.

rationales.water: Dnipro reservoir cascade, though the Kakhovka collapse disrupted downstream balance.
rationales.food: Steppe chernozem plus Kirovohrad's grain belt keep the region a net producer.
rationales.energy: Zaporizhzhia NPP occupied and offline - a national-scale loss; hydro dams and thermal plants damaged.

sources: IAEA reporting on Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant status
Kyiv School of Economics regional war-damage assessments

pole.note: Polycentric industrial belt along the lower Dnipro: Dnipro (largest), Zaporizhzhia and Kryvyi Rih each anchor a distinct industrial complex; Kropyvnytskyi joins as the steppe-agricultural fourth center.

parliament.note: No regional legislature; oblast councils (oblasna rada) are organs of local self-government under Ukraine's unitary constitution, not parliaments.

conflict_flags.description: The Russian Federation unilaterally annexed Crimea (Autonomous Republic of Crimea + Sevastopol) in March 2014 following an internationally unrecognised referendum; the UN General Assembly (Resolution 68/262) and the vast majority of states continue to recognise Crimea as Ukrainian sovereign territory under military occupation. Included here on that basis, with occupation status flagged as an independently toggleable layer.

regions.name: Crimea
regions.identity_basis: Autonomous Republic of Crimea plus the separately-administered city of Sevastopol; historic homeland of the Crimean Tatars (deported en masse by Stalin in 1944, partial return since the 1990s) alongside a Russian-speaking majority population; internationally recognised as Ukrainian territory but under Russian military occupation and unilateral annexation since March 2014.
key_industries: naval/military (Sevastopol, historic Black Sea Fleet base)
regions.population_note: 2014 Ukrainian State Statistics Service estimate (last pre-occupation figure). Russian occupation authorities report different, contested figures reflecting large-scale demographic change (Russian in-migration, Crimean Tatar and pro-Ukrainian emigration) since 2014 that Ukraine and most of the international community do not recognise as valid census data.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Simferopol, regional administrative centre, ~340k
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: tourism, viticulture, naval/military, agriculture (pre-occupation baseline)
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: layered Crimean Tatar/Russian-speaking/Ukrainian identity; occupation has suppressed the region's dependent (non-separatist) status as recognised under Ukrainian sovereignty

regions.nuts1_disagreement: SR2024 Macroregion 04 (UA4) groups Crimea/Sevastopol with Odesa/Mykolaiv/Kherson; split out here as its own region given its distinct occupied status since 2014 (eight years before the rest of southern Ukraine came under partial occupation) and its historically separate Autonomous Republic status (1991-2014) within Ukraine.

autarky.rationale: Chronic water crisis since Ukraine severed the North Crimean Canal in 2014 (partially restored by Russia post-2022 occupation of the Kherson canal source, but precarious); moderate agriculture/viticulture; occupied status creates data/access limitations, so scores are approximate, extrapolated from pre-2014 baselines adjusted for the known canal disruption.

rationales.water: Chronically water-scarce; dependent on the North Crimean Canal (weaponised since 2014).
rationales.food: Dry-steppe agriculture and viticulture; irrigation-dependent.
rationales.energy: Isolated from Ukraine's grid since occupation; supplied from Russia.

sources: OHCHR human rights monitoring reports on occupied Crimea

pole.note: Simferopol is the administrative hub; Sevastopol a separate naval city.

parliament.note: Under Ukrainian law an Autonomous Republic with its own constitution and (suspended) Verkhovna Rada of Crimea; under occupation since 2014, so no legitimate regional legislature currently functions.

conflict_flags.description: Transnistria (Pridnestrovian Moldavian Republic), a strip of territory on the east bank of the Dniester river (~4,163 km2, ~350,000-370,000 residents per its own unrecognised authorities), has functioned as a de facto independent, Russian-garrisoned state since a 1990-92 war, recognised by no UN member state. No NUTS/CNTR sub-geometry exists to map it separately from Moldova's single CNTR country polygon, so this flag is descriptive only and will not produce a distinct shape on conflicts.geojson (documented data limitation).

regions.name: Moldova
regions.identity_basis: Single sovereign state, modelled as one unit given CNTR-only geometry (no NUTS subdivision). Romanian-speaking majority with a historic Bessarabian identity shaped by Russian/Soviet then Romanian then Soviet rule; the Transnistrian breakaway region (east bank of the Dniester) has functioned as an unrecognised de facto state since 1990.
regions.population_note: National Bureau of Statistics of the Republic of Moldova (NBS), 2023 estimate for government-controlled territory (~2.44M), excluding Transnistria. Transnistrian authorities separately report ~350,000-370,000 residents, bringing a combined estimate to roughly 2.8M, though Transnistrian figures are not independently verified. Heavy outward labour emigration (EU, Russia) affects both figures.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Chișinău, metro ~700k, national capital and cultural/economic centre
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: wine, agriculture, textiles, light manufacturing, a growing IT sector
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: single sovereign state, not a sub-national region; modelled as one unit purely because CNTR geometry provides no internal subdivision (see Global Constraints geometry-source list)

autarky.rationale: Fertile black-soil agriculture and viticulture support strong food self-sufficiency, but Moldova is critically energy-import-dependent (historically reliant on Transnistria's Cuciurgan power station and Russian gas transiting Ukraine, a supply that ended in January 2025), and its light-industrial/clothing base remains modest post-Soviet.

rationales.water: Dnister and Prut abstraction adequate but pollution-stressed.
rationales.food: Chernozem-based agriculture (wine, fruit, grain) is the economy's backbone.
rationales.energy: Nearly all gas historically imported; MGRES power plant sits in breakaway Transnistria.

sources: National Bureau of Statistics of the Republic of Moldova, 2023 population estimate
International Crisis Group reporting on Transnistria
IEA/Energy Community Secretariat reporting on Moldova's energy dependence

pole.note: Chisinau is the single dominant urban center of the state.

parliament.name: Parliament of the Republic of Moldova
parliament.note: Sovereign state modelled as one unit; national unicameral legislature.

conflict_flags.description: Abkhazia (~8,600 km2, ~245,000 residents) and South Ossetia/the Tskhinvali Region (~3,900 km2, ~30,000 residents) declared independence and have functioned as de facto states under Russian military protection since the 1992-93 and 2008 conflicts respectively; recognised by Russia and a small number of other states but not by Georgia or the great majority of the UN. No NUTS/CNTR sub-geometry exists to map them separately from Georgia's single CNTR country polygon (documented data limitation, consistent with the Moldova/Transnistria treatment).

regions.name: Georgia
regions.identity_basis: Single sovereign state, modelled as one unit given CNTR-only geometry. Distinct Georgian language/script (not Indo-European) and Georgian Orthodox Christian identity dating to the 4th century; Abkhazia and South Ossetia are de facto independent following the 2008 Russo-Georgian war.
regions.population_note: National Statistics Office of Georgia (Geostat), 2023 estimate (~3.7M) for territory under Tbilisi's control, excluding Abkhazia and South Ossetia. Long-term emigration since the 1990s has substantially reduced Georgia's population from a Soviet-era peak of over 5M.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Tbilisi, metro ~1.2M, national capital and cultural/economic centre
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: viticulture, agriculture, tourism, hydropower, mining
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: single sovereign state; modelled as one unit purely because CNTR geometry provides no internal subdivision

autarky.rationale: Abundant mountain-river hydropower and water resources plus historically strong wine/fruit/tea agriculture drive the higher water and food scores; industrial and clothing/textile bases remain comparatively modest, and Abkhazia/South Ossetia's de facto separation removes meaningful territory and resources from Tbilisi's effective control.

rationales.water: Caucasus rivers give one of Europe's richest per-capita water endowments.
rationales.food: Diverse subtropical-to-alpine agriculture; net importer of grain.
rationales.energy: Hydro covers most electricity; gas imported (Azerbaijan).

sources: National Statistics Office of Georgia (Geostat), 2023 population estimate
International Crisis Group reporting on Abkhazia/South Ossetia
Georgian Ministry of Energy hydropower capacity reports

pole.note: Tbilisi dominates; Batumi and Kutaisi are secondary.

parliament.name: Parliament of Georgia (Sakartvelos Parlamenti)
parliament.note: Sovereign state modelled as one unit; national unicameral legislature.

regions.name: Andorra
regions.identity_basis: Single-unit exception microstate; a co-principality since 1278 (shared sovereignty of the President of France and the Bishop of Urgell), with a distinct Catalan-speaking Pyrenean identity.
regions.population_note: Departament d'Estadística d'Andorra, 2023 estimate (~80,000), of whom a large share are foreign-born residents/workers.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Andorra la Vella, national capital, ~23k, sole urban/administrative centre
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: tourism, duty-free retail, banking - narrow but genuinely diversified within a microstate economy
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: single-unit exception microstate per Global Constraints; sovereign co-principality, not a sub-national region

autarky.rationale: Alpine Pyrenean water supply is ample, but negligible arable land forces near-total food imports; strong healthcare/hygiene from high per-capita income; virtually no domestic clothing manufacturing; a tourism/banking economy leaves little energy self-sufficiency.

rationales.water: Pyrenean headwaters give ample supply.
rationales.food: Negligible arable land; near-total import dependence.
rationales.energy: Small hydro covers a fraction; electricity imported from ES/FR.

pole.note: Single urban valley; the capital and Escaldes-Engordany form one continuous center.

parliament.name: Consell General d'Andorra
parliament.note: Sovereign co-principality; the Consell General (est. 1419) is among Europe's oldest continuous parliaments.

regions.name: Monaco
regions.identity_basis: Single-unit exception microstate; sovereign principality since 1297 under the House of Grimaldi; the densest sovereign state in the world, entirely urbanised.
regions.population_note: IMSEE (Monaco statistics institute), 2023 estimate (~39,150); over half of residents are foreign nationals.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Monaco-Ville/Monte Carlo - the entire state is one contiguous urban centre
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: banking, casino/tourism, real estate, luxury services - a dense service economy
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: single-unit exception microstate; sovereign principality, not a sub-national region

autarky.rationale: Entirely reclaimed/built-up urban territory (2.1 km2) leaves no room for food, energy, or housing self-sufficiency, and it imports essentially everything; world-class private healthcare (a wealthy resident base) is the sole standout dimension.

rationales.water: Supplied via French networks and local desalination; no autonomous source.
rationales.food: Zero agriculture on 2.1 km2 of built-up land.
rationales.energy: Entirely dependent on the French grid.

sources: IMSEE (Institut Monegasque de la Statistique), 2023 population estimate
Monaco Government Tourism and Economic Development reports

pole.note: The entire state is one urban center.

parliament.name: Conseil National de Monaco
parliament.note: Sovereign principality; elected Conseil National shares legislative power with the Prince.

regions.name: San Marino
regions.identity_basis: Single-unit exception microstate; claims to be the world's oldest surviving republic (founded 301 CE per tradition); fully enclaved within Italy, with a distinct Sammarinese civic identity.
regions.population_note: Ufficio di Stato per l'Informatica e le Statistica di San Marino, 2023 estimate (~34,000).

inclusion_test.urban_hub: City of San Marino (hilltop capital) and Serravalle (largest settlement/commercial centre)
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: tourism, banking, ceramics/textiles, collectibles
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: single-unit exception microstate; sovereign republic enclaved within Italy, not a sub-national region

autarky.rationale: A hilltop enclave surrounded entirely by Italy with minimal arable land forces heavy food imports; healthcare integrated with the Italian system supports the hygiene score; a modest historic textile/ceramics industry keeps clothing above the microstate floor.

rationales.water: No significant own catchment; supplied through Italian networks.
rationales.food: Minimal arable land on Monte Titano's slopes.
rationales.energy: Fully dependent on the Italian grid.

sources: Ufficio di Stato per l'Informatica e le Statistica (San Marino), 2023 population estimate
Eurostat correspondence data for San Marino

pole.note: Hilltop capital plus Serravalle below form the single center of the enclave.

parliament.name: Consiglio Grande e Generale
parliament.note: Sovereign republic; 60-member Grand and General Council, continuous since the medieval Arengo.

regions.name: Vatican City
regions.name_local: Città del Vaticano / Status Civitatis Vaticanae
regions.identity_basis: Single-unit exception microstate; the world's smallest sovereign state (0.49 km2), seat of the Holy See and the Roman Catholic Church since 1929 (Lateran Treaty); population consists almost entirely of clergy, Swiss Guards, and Curia staff rather than an ordinary resident population.
regions.population_note: Approximate resident population per Holy See press office figures (~800, overwhelmingly clergy and Swiss Guard); a separate, smaller cohort (~450) hold Vatican citizenship, which is granted by office and lapses on leaving that office rather than by birth or residence.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Vatican City itself - the entire state is one urban/ecclesiastical precinct
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: religious administration, museums/tourism, publishing - narrow by design, not a general economy
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: single-unit exception microstate; sovereign city-state, not a sub-national region

autarky.rationale: Entirely import-dependent enclave within Rome with zero agriculture or industry; even water and electricity are supplied via Italian infrastructure agreements; included per the brief's instruction to score Food 1 for the world's smallest sovereign state.

rationales.water: Water supplied by Rome's utility under the Lateran Treaty arrangements.
rationales.food: Zero agriculture; fully import-dependent.
rationales.energy: Electricity supplied via Italian infrastructure agreements.

sources: Holy See Press Office population/citizenship figures
Lateran Treaty (1929) territorial and status provisions

pole.note: The entire state is one ecclesiastical precinct.

parliament.note: Legislative power rests with the appointed Pontifical Commission for Vatican City State - an absolute elective monarchy, not a parliament.

regions.name: Cossack Hetmanate (Left-Bank Ukraine)
regions.identity_basis: Heartland of the Cossack Hetmanate (1649-1764), the autonomous Cossack polity founded by Bohdan Khmelnytskyi that anchors modern Ukrainian national historiography: Poltava and Chernihiv formed its Left-Bank regimental core (capitals at Baturyn and Hlukhiv in Chernihiv land), while Cherkasy - though on the Right Bank - was the original Cossack cradle, holding Khmelnytskyi's capital Chyhyryn and the Kholodnyi Yar insurgent tradition. A shared regimental-town heritage, baroque church landscape ('Cossack baroque'), and the Poltava dialect basis of literary Ukrainian bind the three oblasts.
regions.population_note: Sum of 2021 Ukrstat oblast estimates: Poltava (~1.37M) + Cherkasy (~1.18M) + Chernihiv (~0.98M). Chernihiv oblast suffered heavy 2022 invasion damage in its north; displacement not reflected in this baseline.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Poltava (~280k) is the largest center and historic-symbolic anchor; stated honestly, this is a three-oblast region of mid-size regimental towns rather than a single-metro region
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: chernozem grain/sugar agriculture, Ukraine's main onshore oil-and-gas basin (Poltava), Kremenchuk's refinery and vehicle plants, food processing
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: the Hetmanate legacy is the founding myth of modern Ukrainian statehood - an identity emphatically within, indeed constitutive of, Ukraine; no separatism

regions.nuts1_disagreement: SR2024 places Poltava and Cherkasy in macroregion UA9 with Kirovohrad, and Chernihiv in UAA with Sumy/Kharkiv; this region instead unites the three historic Hetmanate-core oblasts, re-homing Kirovohrad to the Dnipro industrial-steppe region (Zaporozhian free-lands heritage, Kryvyi Rih economic ties) and leaving Sumy with Slobozhanshchyna where its settlement history belongs.

autarky.rationale: Prime chernozem agriculture and Ukraine's principal domestic gas basin give strong food and fair energy standing; the Dnipro and Kremenchuk reservoir anchor water; dispersed mid-size towns keep transport and services moderate.

rationales.water: Dnipro river frontage with the Kremenchuk reservoir plus Desna/Vorskla basins.
rationales.food: Core chernozem belt: grain, sugar beet and dairy make this one of Ukraine's strongest food-surplus areas.
rationales.energy: Poltava oblast hosts most of Ukraine's domestic gas production and the Kremenchuk refinery (war-damaged); still short of full self-supply.

sources: Eurostat/GISCO SR2024 non-EU statistical regions documentation

pole.note: Three regimental-heritage oblast capitals of similar order; Poltava listed central as the largest and the region's historic-symbolic anchor.

parliament.note: No regional legislature; oblast councils (oblasna rada) are organs of local self-government under Ukraine's unitary constitution, not parliaments.

regions.name: Podillia
regions.identity_basis: Historic Podillia (Podolia): the upland between the Dnister and Southern Buh, a distinct named land since the 14th century (Podolian Voivodeship under Poland-Lithuania, later Podolia Governorate), with its emblematic fortress capital Kamianets-Podilskyi. Right-Bank agrarian Ukraine shaped by Polish-Lithuanian landlord heritage, dense small-town (shtetl) history, and the Podillian dialect group; today organized by Vinnytsia, one of Ukraine's fastest-modernising mid-size cities, with Khmelnytskyi as second pole.
regions.population_note: Sum of 2021 Ukrstat oblast estimates: Vinnytsia (~1.53M) + Khmelnytskyi (~1.24M). A significant IDP destination since 2022; current population likely exceeds this baseline.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Vinnytsia (~370k) - the region's dominant city and a national model of municipal reform
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: sugar/grain/fruit agribusiness, major food-processing plants, the Khmelnytskyi nuclear power plant, growing logistics role on the western corridors
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: Podillia is one of Ukraine's oldest named historic lands, an identity fully within Ukraine; no separatism

regions.nuts1_disagreement: SR2024 macroregion UA5 groups Vinnytsia and Khmelnytskyi with Ternopil; Ternopil sits in ua-lviv-galicia here (its Galician history under Austria diverges from Podillia's Russian-imperial governorate history), so this region is UA5 minus Ternopil.

autarky.rationale: Chernozem agribusiness surplus plus the Khmelnytskyi nuclear plant (with expansion under way) make Podillia unusually self-sufficient in both food and electricity; the Dnister/Buh uplands secure water; rail links to the EU corridors are improving from a modest base.

rationales.water: Dnister and Southern Buh headwater uplands with reliable flow.
rationales.food: Ukraine's sugar-beet heartland with strong grain, fruit and poultry output - clear surplus producer.
rationales.energy: Khmelnytskyi NPP (2 operating units, 2 more under construction) plus Dnister-basin hydro nearby make the region a net electricity exporter.

sources: Eurostat/GISCO SR2024 non-EU statistical regions documentation

pole.note: Two oblast capitals of the same order; Vinnytsia is the clearly stronger organizing center, Khmelnytskyi the western counterweight.

parliament.note: No regional legislature; oblast councils (oblasna rada) are organs of local self-government under Ukraine's unitary constitution, not parliaments.

regions.name: Volhynia and Polissia
regions.identity_basis: Historic Volhynia - a named land since Kyivan Rus (Volodymyr-Volynskyi principality), later the Volhynian Voivodeship and Governorate - together with the Polissia woodland belt that stretches east across Zhytomyr. Flat glacial lowlands of forest, marsh and lakes distinct from both Galicia's Austrian heritage to the south and the chernozem steppe to the east; the Volhynian and Polissian dialect groups, a Polish-Czech-German settlement layer, and the interwar Polish/Soviet border experience mark the region. Lutsk (historic Volhynian capital) and Rivne form the western core, Zhytomyr the eastern Polissian extension.
regions.population_note: Sum of 2021 Ukrstat oblast estimates: Volyn (~1.03M) + Rivne (~1.15M) + Zhytomyr (~1.20M).

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Lutsk (~220k, historic Volhynian capital) with Rivne (~245k) as near-equal twin; stated honestly a polycentric region of mid-size capitals rather than a single-metro region
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: Rivne nuclear plant, Polissia timber industry, flax/hops/dairy farming, amber, border-corridor logistics toward Poland
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: Volhynian identity is a historic-land identity fully within Ukraine; no separatism

regions.nuts1_disagreement: Matches SR2024 macroregion UA8 (Volyn, Rivne, Zhytomyr) exactly - the only one of the three ua-central-podillia successor regions that coincides with an SR macroregion; named here for the historic land rather than the statistical code.

autarky.rationale: Polissia's water and timber wealth, solid mixed farming on sandier soils, and the Rivne nuclear plant give balanced self-sufficiency; Chornobyl-zone contamination in eastern Zhytomyr and modest road/rail density hold back the top scores.

rationales.water: Pripyat-basin lakes, marshes and rivers make this Ukraine's most water-abundant belt.
rationales.food: Flax, hops, potato and dairy farming on Polissian soils - a solid producer, below chernozem-belt yields.
rationales.energy: Rivne NPP (4 units) makes the region a large net electricity exporter.

sources: Eurostat/GISCO SR2024 non-EU statistical regions documentation

pole.note: Three mid-size oblast capitals; Lutsk listed central as the historic Volhynian capital, with Rivne its near-equal twin and Zhytomyr anchoring eastern Polissia.

parliament.note: No regional legislature; oblast councils (oblasna rada) are organs of local self-government under Ukraine's unitary constitution, not parliaments.

conflict_flags.description: The September 2023 Azerbaijani offensive ended the Nagorno-Karabakh Armenian polity; over 100,000 ethnic Armenians fled to Armenia within weeks - roughly 3% added to the state's population - and Armenia-Azerbaijan border demarcation remains contested with recurring armed incidents. Flag covers the displacement burden and unsettled border, not any territorial claim rendered on this map.

regions.name: Armenia
regions.identity_basis: Sovereign republic modelled as a single unit (scope amendment alongside Georgia): the world's oldest Christian state (301 CE), with its own alphabet (Mashtots, 405 CE) and a language forming its own branch of Indo-European; a highland nation defined by the Ararat plain, a worldwide diaspora larger than the home population, and the post-2020/2023 loss of Nagorno-Karabakh reshaping national identity.
key_industries: IT and software services (a leading post-Soviet tech hub)
regions.population_note: Armstat estimate ~2.99M (early 2024), including the ~100k ethnic-Armenian refugees who arrived from Nagorno-Karabakh in late 2023.

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Yerevan - capital, ~1.1M, over a third of the state's population and its single dominant center
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: copper/molybdenum mining, a genuinely strong IT-services sector, food/brandy processing, tourism, remittance economy
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: sovereign state modelled as one unit at the dataset's edge, like Georgia and Moldova; internal regions (marzer) have no separate political identities of the kind this map tracks

regions.nuts1_disagreement: Outside the NUTS classification; geometry via the GISCO CNTR countries file (CNTR_ID 'AM'), following the Moldova/Georgia precedent for non-EU eastern-partnership states in scope.

autarky.rationale: Highland water and the Metsamor nuclear plant plus hydro give fair basics, but a landlocked position with two of four borders (Turkey, Azerbaijan) closed cripples transport, and food/energy still lean on imports through Georgia and Iran.

rationales.water: Highland catchments and Lake Sevan give ample water, though Sevan's level is managed under stress.
rationales.food: Ararat-plain orchards/vineyards and livestock cover part of demand; grain largely imported (historically from Russia).
rationales.energy: Metsamor NPP (~30-40% of electricity) plus hydro; all gas imported (Russia via Georgia, Iran swap).

sources: Armstat (Statistical Committee of Armenia), 2024 population estimate

pole.note: Extreme capital primacy: Yerevan holds over a third of the national population.

parliament.name: National Assembly (Azgayin Zhoghov)
parliament.note: Sovereign state modelled as one unit; national unicameral legislature.

regions.name: East Thrace
regions.identity_basis: The European-continent portion of Turkey west of Istanbul province (Tekirdağ, Edirne, Kırklareli): Ottoman Rumelia's remnant, with Edirne (Adrianople) a former Ottoman capital and seat of Sinan's Selimiye Mosque, a Thracian-plain agricultural identity shared with Greek and Bulgarian Thrace across the borders, and an industrial corridor (Çorlu-Çerkezköy) functioning as Istanbul's overspill zone. SPECIAL NOTE: Turkey is excluded from this dataset as a whole; this unit is included solely so the European landmass is covered without a hole west of Istanbul - its presence implies no position on Turkey's inclusion otherwise (Istanbul province itself, though partly European, is excluded with the rest of Turkey).
regions.population_note: TurkStat 2023 province estimates: Tekirdağ (~1.14M) + Edirne (~0.42M) + Kırklareli (~0.37M).

inclusion_test.urban_hub: Tekirdağ (~1.1M province anchored by the Tekirdağ-Çorlu urban belt) - though the region's true metropolis, Istanbul, lies just outside its (and the dataset's) boundary
inclusion_test.diversified_industry: one of Turkey's densest textile/leather manufacturing zones, Thracian-plain export agriculture, wine, trans-border logistics
inclusion_test.dependent_identity: Rumelian/Thracian identity within Turkey; included for landmass completeness, not as a statement on Turkish regionalism

regions.nuts1_disagreement: NUTS-1 TR2 (Batı Marmara) also contains TR22 (Balıkesir, Çanakkale) on the Anatolian side of the straits; only TR21 - the purely European portion - is included, since the dataset's coverage rule concerns the European landmass and Turkey is otherwise out of scope.

autarky.rationale: The Thracian plain's grain/sunflower surplus and the Çorlu textile complex give strong food and clothing scores - the latter the dataset's rare textile-self-sufficiency case; the E80/rail corridor to Istanbul and Europe carries transport; water is adequate but strained by industry.

rationales.water: Ergene basin supplies the plain but suffers heavy industrial pollution; Istranca reservoirs supplement.
rationales.food: Turkey's sunflower heartland with strong wheat and rice (Meriç) output - a clear surplus producer.
rationales.energy: Hamitabat gas-fired plant and growing wind capacity on the Thracian ridges; still a net importer.

sources: Trakya Development Agency (Trakya Kalkınma Ajansı) regional reports
regions.special_status: out-of-scope-state landmass inclusion (Turkey excluded as a whole; East Thrace shown for European landmass completeness)

pole.note: Tekirdağ anchors the industrial-demographic east, Edirne the historic-cultural west (former Ottoman capital); the region's actual gravitational center, Istanbul, lies outside the dataset.

reach.note: The region functions substantially within Istanbul's catchment - the Çorlu-Çerkezköy zone is Istanbul-overspill industry and the E80/rail corridor ties the plain to the metropolis - but Istanbul province is excluded with the rest of Turkey.

parliament.note: No regional legislature; Turkish provinces are centrally administered (appointed governors plus elected provincial councils with limited powers).

notes: Region-count tension (updated for draft_v0.1.2): v0.1.0 authored 31 zone-1 records by honoring 18 mandated German splits, 5 mandated Austrian regions (with Carinthia folded into Styria and Salzburg folded into Upper Austria for parsimony), 6 Swiss macro-regions (with Schaffhausen folded into Central & Eastern CH), Liechtenstein, and the tyrol-unified variant. draft_v0.1.2's content wave undoes four of those parsimony merges under the explicit parliament rule and historical-founding mandates: Styria != Carinthia, Salzburg != Upper Austria, Rhineland-Palatinate != Saarland, Berlin != Brandenburg, and Schaffhausen != Central & Eastern Switzerland. Combined with three new hidden (default_visible false) variant-view records (at-vienna-danube-extended, ch-central-eastern-combined, plus three Lower-Saxony/Bremen variant records) needed to power the new variant sets, zone1 now totals 41 records: 35 default_visible=true cultural units plus 6 default_visible=false alternate-view records. This again mirrors the project's own 40-70-vs-90-110 tension: honoring every explicitly named v0.1.2 split pushes the visible count from 31 to 35 before any variant-set scaffolding is added. Flagged rather than silently smoothed over, per the project's standing convention.

Lower Saxony vs Saxony nuance (still valid, unchanged by v0.1.2): despite the near-homophone English names, Niedersachsen (Lower Saxony) and Sachsen (Saxony) are historically and dialectally unrelated -- Lower Saxony descends from the medieval Duchy of Saxony's north-western Low German-speaking remnant, while modern Sachsen descends from the Wettin Margraviate of Meissen/Kingdom of Saxony, an East Central German-speaking territory that inherited the 'Saxon' name through a 12th-century dynastic transfer of title, not linguistic-territorial continuity. Both remain separate regions here; each region's nuts1_disagreement field flags the naming confusion explicitly.

Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern inclusion-test honesty check (still valid, unchanged by v0.1.2): Saxony-Anhalt is the weaker case -- a 1947 administrative creation (Prussian Saxony province + Anhalt duchy) with no deep pre-existing regional unity, dissolved entirely under the GDR's Bezirke system 1952-90, and only reconstituted in 1990. It is nonetheless kept as its own region on the strength of its genuine post-1990 civic identity, urban hub (Halle/Magdeburg) and diversified industrial base. Mecklenburg-Vorpommern passes more comfortably (Rostock hub, 1945 merger of historically related Low-German duchies, genuinely diversified tourism/shipbuilding/offshore-wind base).

Parliament rule applied (draft_v0.1.2, new): the plan mandates that any region with its own parliament gets its own cultural unit. This directly resolved three v0.1.0 parsimony merges that the original file had explicitly flagged as open tensions: Rhineland-Palatinate (own Landtag, Mainz) is now split from Saarland (own Landtag, Saarbruecken); Berlin (own Abgeordnetenhaus) is now split from Brandenburg (own Landtag, Potsdam) -- honoring the 1996 merger referendum's failure. Where a Land-level parliament still does NOT map 1:1 onto a cultural unit -- Bavaria's Landtag governing Franconia/Bavarian-Swabia/Altbayern as three separate cultural units; NRW's Landtag governing Rhineland/Westphalia as two; Baden-Wuerttemberg's Landtag governing Baden/Wuerttemberg as two; the Vienna-East record combining three distinct Austrian Landtage (Vienna, Lower Austria, Burgenland); and all multi-canton Swiss groupings (Basel, Bern-Mittelland, Romandie, Central & Eastern CH) each combining several cantonal parliaments -- each such record's `parliament` field carries `has_own: false` plus a note naming the actual body/bodies, so the parliament_exceptions audit can enumerate them explicitly rather than the data silently implying a false 1:1 mapping. Single-canton Swiss units (Zuerich, Ticino, and the newly split Schaffhausen) correctly carry `has_own: true`, since for those the cultural unit and the parliament's jurisdiction already coincide.

Schaffhausen split (draft_v0.1.2, new): Schaffhausen (SR2024 CH052) is split out of the former ch-central-eastern combination per its distinct 1501 Confederacy-accession history and its near-exclave geography (surrounded by Germany on three sides), rather than remaining an undifferentiated part of the broad Zentral-/Ostschweiz statistical grouping. The v0.1.0 combined framing is preserved as a default_visible-false alternate view (ch-central-eastern-combined) for the new schaffhausen variant set, alongside a 'separate' default view and an 'overlap' view.

Upper Austria / Vienna variant set (draft_v0.1.2, new): now that Salzburg and Upper Austria are split into separate cultural units, a new upper-austria variant set offers an alternative 'vienna-join' view in which Upper Austria's Danube-valley economy is shown merged with Vienna & Eastern Austria (at-vienna-danube-extended, default_visible false) rather than standing alone, reflecting the real Vienna-Linz Danube-corridor economic axis without claiming shared cultural identity.

Lower Saxony + Bremen variant set merged into one (draft_v0.1.2, new): the plan named these as two separate mandated variant sets (lower-saxony: together/west-east-split; bremen: Lower-Saxony-united/west-east-split/overlap), but both sets would toggle visibility on the same underlying de-lower-saxony/de-bremen records, which would produce conflicting view states if kept as two independent sets. They are merged here into one bremen-lower-saxony variant set with four views (together / split / united / overlap), documented in data/variant_sets/zone1.json. The 'split' view divides Lower Saxony into de-lower-saxony-west (Weser-Ems, DE94, urban core Oldenburg) and de-lower-saxony-east (Braunschweig+Hannover+Lueneburg, DE91-93, urban core Hannover); Lueneburg (DE93) is assigned to the eastern half (it lies geographically east of the Bremen enclave, between Hamburg and Hannover) so the two halves sum exactly to Lower Saxony's full NUTS-2 coverage rather than leaving a coverage gap.

Carinthia (draft_v0.1.2 UPDATE -- supersedes the v0.1.0 merge note): Carinthia (AT21) is now split out of the former at-styria-carinthia combination as its own cultural unit (at-carinthia), honoring its distinct Kaerntnerisch dialect, Alpine-lake tourism economy and constitutionally recognized Slovene-speaking minority, per the draft_v0.1.2 content-wave mandate. The v0.1.0 merge-for-parsimony is no longer in effect.

Salzburg (draft_v0.1.2 UPDATE -- supersedes the v0.1.0 merge note): Salzburg (AT32) is now split out of the former at-salzburg-upper-austria combination as its own cultural unit (at-salzburg), honoring its distinct history as an independent Prince-Archbishopric until 1803/1816, per the draft_v0.1.2 content-wave mandate.

Switzerland's Central & Eastern region (ch-central-eastern) remains a deliberately broad combination of the historic Zentralschweiz founding cantons with the remaining Ostschweiz cantons (Schaffhausen now split out separately, see above); the internal heterogeneity (Zug's finance-haven status, Graubuenden's trilingual Romansh-speaking Alpine identity) is genuine and is not resolved here, flagged as a candidate for future subdivision.

Bern-Mittelland linguistic frontier (still valid, unchanged by v0.1.2): the Swiss statistical macro-region 'Espace Mittelland' (Bern, Fribourg, Solothurn, Neuchatel, Jura) is German-plurality but includes two fully francophone cantons (Neuchatel, Jura) and one bilingual canton (Fribourg/Freiburg); the Roestigraben (German/French linguistic boundary) runs through this region. Modeled as an independently toggleable conflict_flag (bern-mittelland-linguistic-frontier) on the ch-bern-mittelland record.

Vorarlberg's Alemannic dialect continuum and dual Swiss-Tyrolean orientation (draft_v0.1.2 UPDATE): Vorarlberg's Alemannic dialect continuum (conflict_flag vorarlberg-alemannic-continuum) links it culturally to eastern Switzerland, southern Baden and Alsace. draft_v0.1.2 additionally adds a mandated `special_status: "dual Swiss+Tyrolean orientation"` field: the linguistic/cultural pull is Swiss-Alemannic (not Austro-Bavarian like the rest of Austria), while administratively and historically Vorarlberg was long paired with Tyrol (shared judiciary and Statthalterei arrangements before 1918, both grouped under NUTS-1 AT3 Westoesterreich today) -- a genuine dual orientation, not a single clean affiliation.

Tyrol congruence toggle (still valid, unchanged by v0.1.2): at-tyrol (AT33, default_visible true) is authored here; the corresponding South Tyrol congruent record (ITH1, Provincia Autonoma di Bolzano/Bozen) is authored in zone3. The tyrol-unified record (AT33 + ITH1, default_visible false) is authored here and legitimately reuses AT33 already claimed by at-tyrol, since default_visible-false alternate-view records are exempted from the code-overlap check (which is scoped to default_visible-true records only).

Liechtenstein special_status (draft_v0.1.2, new): added to the schema-v2 mandated dashed-stroke list as 'sovereign microstate', for visual parity with Vatican/Monaco/Andorra/San Marino elsewhere in the dataset. Berlin and Bremen additionally carry `special_status: "city-state"` (alongside the mandated Hamburg) for parallelism among Germany's three Stadtstaaten -- an editorial extension beyond the literal Hamburg-only mandate, noted here rather than silently added.

Groupings tension (draft_v0.1.2, new; see data/groupings/zone1.json + zone4.json): the plan's guidance suggests ~12-16 representation groupings across zone1+zone4 combined, out of a project-wide 40-70 target. Zone1+zone4 together hold roughly 60 of the project's ~191 default-visible cultural units (~31%), which proportionally implies something closer to 12-22 groupings at the 40-70 project range -- but honoring distinct linguistic/cantonal/national identities (e.g. not merging Ticino with Romandie, not merging the Baltic states with Nordic islands purely to hit a number) produced 14 zone1 groupings + 16 zone4 groupings = 30 total. This is flagged explicitly for the controller/audit rather than forced down via incoherent cross-identity merges, consistent with the project's standing convention of stating such tensions rather than silently truncating.
